title: A Gaussian Process State Space Formulation for Materials Constitutive Modeling: Application to Quasi-brittle Materials

paper.title: A Gaussian Process State Space Formulation for Materials Constitutive Modeling: Application to Quasi-brittle Materials
paper.abstract:
Abstract Constitutive models for history-dependent, path-dependent materials typically encode this dependence in prescribed functional forms through internal variables such as damage or plastic strain that are phenomenological, model-dependent, and not directly observable. These rigid functional forms lack flexibility to match observations, make calibration potentially non-unique, and complicate uncertainty quantification and propagation through finite element predictions. This paper develops a Gaussian-process state-space model (GP-SSM) that replaces the fixed form of the constitutive model with a flexible GP regression, and the prescribed internal variables with a set of latent state variables learned directly from observable stress–strain histories. As a GP, the model is naturally endowed with a measure of uncertainty and can be constrained to satisfy necessary physical principles. We demonstrate this framework for quasi-brittle materials under triaxial compression, where the latent variable evolution is driven by the current-state stress invariants and the increment of equivalent strain
to reflect the evolution of irreversible, pressure-sensitive history. A sparse multi-output Gaussian process then maps the latent state and current strain tensor to the six-component stress response. Variational sparse inference enables tractable training from sequential stress-strain data that retains a probabilistic structure for offline uncertainty assessment.
The trained model is exported into Abaqus/Explicit through a user material subroutine.
Four verification cases are reported: (1) offline full-sequence rollout evaluation on the validation and test histories; (2) a single element simulation under changing confinement, which exercises the complete Abaqus/Explicit deployment pathway; (3) a frozen-memory unloading–reloading extension in which latent evolution stops once equivalent strain recedes below its historical maximum; and (4) a multi-element structural model that reproduces a loading condition from the Karagozian and Case Concrete (KCC) model and is compared directly against KCC as a reference solution.
These results show that the learned state-space update (i) reproduces held-out RVE-scale histories in closed-loop rollout, (ii) can be evaluated incrementally in an explicit finite element solver, (iii) tracks a confining stress that evolves during loading, (iv) supports unloading without violating the irreversibility of the learned history state, and (v) reproduces structural-level compression behavior consistent with an established constitutive model. The framework provides a practical route to bring together probabilistic machine learning, latent internal-state modeling, and finite element-compatible constitutive modeling.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Path-dependent, history-dependent constitutive behavior is difficult to model because the current stress depends not only on the current strain but on the loading path. Classical phenomenological models, including damage mechanics, plasticity, and cap-type formulations, have hypothesized functional forms that represent this path dependence through internal variables whose predictive capability depends strongly on parameters that are difficult to identify uniquely from limited tests. This difficulty is especially pronounced for quasi-brittle materials such as concrete and rock ( Bažant and Planas, 1998 ; Yang et al., 2025 ) , where the macroscopic response is governed by evolving microcracking, frictional sliding, compaction, dilatancy, and confinement-dependent failure. These mechanisms produce nonlinear stiffness degradation, pressure-sensitive strength, path dependence, and post-peak softening. Cap-type formulations such as the Karagozian and Case Concrete (KCC) model ( Malvar et al., 1997 ; Wu and Crawford, 2015 ) have been widely adopted for this material class because they encode mechanics-inspired assumptions and are computationally efficient in finite element solvers, although (like other phenomenological models) they inherit the same difficulty of calibration. The central difficulty is not only that material parameters are uncertain. The internal history variables used by many constitutive theories are not directly measurable in standard stress–strain experiments. Quantities such as damage, plastic strain, hardening, crack-density, or compaction are introduced to make the constitutive update path dependent, but despite their physical interpretability, these variables as typically defined are model-specific and difficult to measure. As a result, calibration often becomes an ill-posed inverse problem: different parameter sets and internal-variable evolutions may reproduce the same observed stress–strain curves while implying different predictions under other loading paths. Replacing such fixed-form models and their prescribed internal variables with a representation learned directly from stress–strain data has a substantial history, dating back to early neural-network constitutive models ( Ghaboussi et al., 1991 ) . Deep-learning surrogates have also been applied directly to confinement-dependent, strain-softening rock behavior under triaxial loading ( Shi et al., 2022 ) . Recent surveys catalog the breadth of data-driven constitutive laws across material classes ( Fuhg et al., 2025 ) . A comprehensive review of these models is beyond the scope of this work. The need for a history-dependent representation of the material state is particularly important for quasi-brittle materials under triaxial compression. Confinement can change both stiffness and strength, while deviatoric loading controls shear-dominated damage and post-peak evolution. Two material points with the same instantaneous strain tensor may therefore correspond to different crack, compaction, and stress-history states. A data-driven material law that predicts stress only from the current strain tensor is unlikely to be robust when embedded in a finite element analysis, where local loading paths are generated by the coupled boundary-value problem rather than prescribed directly from laboratory tests. State-space learning provides a natural way to address this problem. Since the classical Kalman filter ( Kalman, 1960 ) , state-space models have introduced a hidden state that evolves incrementally and summarizes the information needed to predict a system’s future observations; Gaussian-process (GP) and recurrent neural-network extensions of this idea have been used to learn nonlinear latent dynamics directly from sequential data ( Wang et al., 2008 ; Krishnan et al., 2017 ) . In a constitutive setting, such a hidden state can be interpreted as a learned low-dimensional representation of the material history. Note that the hidden state need not be identifiable as the damage, plastic strain, or any particular classical or hypothesized internal variable. However, it serves the same functional role, encoding the essential information from the past that is needed to update the current stress. Moreover, essential physical constraints (e.g. non-negative dissipation) can be placed on these latent variables, and their interpretation may provide important mechanistic insights into material performance. In a related effort, recent work has begun to replace individual phenomenological surfaces within classical concrete models with data-driven models. Li et al. (2026) replace the empirical failure surface of the KCC model with a physics-constrained GP regression surrogate trained on triaxial compression data, and show that embedding known material-property constraints into the GP prior markedly improves accuracy (compared with an unconstrained regressor) and reduces predictive uncertainty and inadmissible material behavior beyond the training confinement range. That work uses a surrogate that replaces a single static failure surface evaluated at a given loading state. This paper develops a Gaussian-process state-space model (GP-SSM) formulation for history-dependent constitutive modeling. The model is specifically applied in the context of quasi-brittle materials, but the framework can be applied broadly to diverse classes of nonlinear history-dependent materials. The model combines three ingredients. First, a low-dimensional latent state represents unobserved material history. In conventional recurrent neural-network surrogates for path-dependent plasticity, the hidden vector plays two roles simultaneously: it propagates the material history forward from one increment to the next, and its size also determines how complex an update the network can represent. A more capable surrogate therefore requires a larger stored state, and such models commonly use comparatively large hidden states ( Mozaffar et al., 2019 ; Gorji et al., 2020 ) . The Minimal State Cell of Bonatti and Mohr (2021) was designed to separate these two roles, so that a wide and deep update network can act on a persistent state of only a few variables. Our model shares this state-parsimony objective. Its persistent memory is restricted to a small, fixed number of latent variables learned directly from stress–strain histories rather than prescribed as phenomenological internal variables. Its distinction lies in combining this compact state with a mechanics-informed evolution. The latent variable evolution is driven by equivalent strain and previous-step stress invariants, introducing mechanics-informed sensitivity to irreversible loading progression, pressure, and deviatoric stress intensity. Then, a sparse multi-output Gaussian process ( Rasmussen and Williams, 2005 ; Álvarez et al., 2012 ) , trained via stochastic variational inference over inducing points ( Titsias, 2009 ; Hensman et al., 2013 ) , maps the latent state and current strain tensor to the six-component stress tensor. This is in contrast to deterministic neural-network stress maps, and follows the general precedent of using Gaussian processes to model latent dynamical systems ( Deisenroth et al., 2015 ) . The Gaussian-process structure provides a nonparametric and data-efficient stress map built from a probabilistic formulation for quantifying uncertainty in the material model and allows offline uncertainty propagation through finite element simulations. A practical objective of this work is finite element compatibility. Data-driven constitutive models are frequently developed and validated as offline regressors. History-dependent machine-learning surrogates that have been embedded directly in finite element solvers have primarily been applied to accelerating multiscale FE 2 homogenization by, e.g., replacing an expensive micro-scale solve with a recurrent-neural-network surrogate ( Ghavamian and Simone, 2019 ) , or by using a trained recurrent network as the homogenized material update itself ( Logarzo et al., 2021 ) . This work demonstrates a full experiment-to-deployment pipeline built as an alternative to phenomenological constitutive models, in which the material model is evaluated locally and incrementally at every integration point, with state variables stored and updated by the solver. Note that although the verification cases in this paper use concrete-like triaxial data and are compared against the KCC model, the mechanics-informed state-space structure of GP-SSM is applicable to other pressure-sensitive, path-dependent quasi-brittle materials such as rocks and ceramics, that share the same broad failure mechanisms ( Bažant and Planas, 1998 ; Li and Ramesh, 2021 ) . The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the elastic-predictor, boundary-correction structure shared by classical plasticity and damage-plasticity models, using the KCC model as a representative example, and highlights the phenomenological cost of designing pressure-dependent failure boundaries explicitly. Section 3 formalizes the latent-state constitutive problem in this alternative setting. Section 4 presents the GP-SSM formulation. Section 5 describes data processing and training. Section 6 reports four verification cases, beginning with offline full-sequence rollout evaluation and proceeding through Abaqus/Explicit material-point and structural simulations. Finally, Sections 7 and 8 discuss limitations and conclusions.

sections.heading: 2.1 Mechanistic, phenomenological, and data-driven modeling
sections.text: Constructing a constitutive model requires developing the stress–strain relation, and its history dependence. Three broad approaches are used in practice. Mechanistic models derive the relation from an explicit subscale mechanism. Phenomenological models instead postulate the relation at the scale of application and calibrate it to fit observed response, without deriving it directly from a lower-scale mechanism. Data-driven models learn the relation directly from stress–strain data, with minimal or no assumed functional form. These labels classify the origins of a modeling approach rather than the model that contains it. A complete constitutive model is typically a composite: it may derive one component from a mechanism, postulate a second, and (particularly recently) learn a third. The three approaches also differ in how much structure is assumed before any data are seen, and that choice involves a consistent trade-off. The more structure a model assumes, the less data it requires and the further it can be trusted outside the conditions on which it was calibrated, but the more its predictions depend on that structure being correct. The mechanistic paradigm is broadly applicable, but any individual mechanistic model is necessarily specific to the material class whose deformation mechanism it encodes. In metals, crystal plasticity derives macroscopic flow directly from dislocation slip on crystallographic slip systems ( Roters et al., 2010 ; Roters et al., 2019 ) . In polymers and elastomers, network theories such as the Arruda–Boyce eight-chain model derive the hyperelastic stress–stretch relation from the statistical mechanics of a network of freely jointed polymer chains ( Arruda and Boyce, 1993 ) . In both cases, the relation follows as a consequence of the assumed lower-scale mechanism rather than as a curve fit to test data, and in both cases the resulting model inherits the scope of that mechanism: slip kinematics has no counterpart in an elastomer network, and vice versa. The mechanistic route is therefore available only where the governing mechanism is both identified and tractably represented at the scale of interest. Phenomenological constitutive models have likewise been developed for a variety of material classes. Mooney–Rivlin hyperelasticity postulates a strain-energy function directly in terms of invariants of the deformation and calibrates its coefficients to (for example) rubber test data ( Mooney, 1940 ; Rivlin, 1948 ) , without deriving that function from a network mechanism. J 2 J_{2} (von Mises) plasticity with isotropic or kinematic hardening postulates a yield surface and hardening law for metals and calibrates them to observed hardening curves ( Lubliner, 2008 ; Simo and Hughes, 1998 ) , without necessarily deriving them from the mechanics of dislocation slip. The boundary between the mechanistic and phenomenological approaches may be softer than the definitions suggest. A postulated form is rarely arbitrary: e.g., J 2 J_{2} plasticity assumes that yielding is insensitive to pressure and to the third invariant, an assumption that is mechanistic in origin, since dislocation slip is volume-preserving. What makes such a model phenomenological is not the absence of mechanistic reasoning, but that the mechanism informs the choice of form rather than supplying it. This mixed character is apparent, for example, in damage or porosity-based constitutive models such as the Gurson-Tvergaard-Needleman (GTN) model ( Gurson, 1977 ; Tvergaard, 1981 ; Tvergaard and Needleman, 1984 ) that hypothesize a pressure-dependent yield function that is porosity dependent and phenomenologically informed by the mechanisms of void nucleation, growth, and coalescence. Data-driven constitutive models learn the relation, or its evolution, directly from observed data (whether measured or generated by simulation) with little or no assumed functional form. Such models differ among themselves chiefly in what is learned. Sequence models learn the incremental update itself, mapping strain history to stress through a recurrent hidden state ( Ghaboussi et al., 1991 ; Mozaffar et al., 2019 ; Gorji et al., 2020 ; Bonatti and Mohr, 2021 ) . Potential-based approaches learn a stored-energy or dissipation function and recover stress by differentiation, so that the learned object is a scalar rather than the stress ( Masi et al., 2021 ; As’ad et al., 2022 ) . Discovery-based approaches learn a sparse, interpretable expression for the law itself, in some cases from full-field displacement and reaction data without stress labels ( Flaschel et al., 2022 ) . Model-free data-driven computing dispenses with a constitutive function altogether, searching a database of observed states ( Kirchdoerfer and Ortiz, 2016 ) or their distribution ( Xu et al., 2024a ) directly; it is less a way of constructing a constitutive relation than a reformulation of the boundary-value problem that avoids needing one. Fuhg et al. (2025) survey this landscape across material classes in far more detail than is attempted here. The microplane model M7 ( Caner and Bažant, 2013a ; Caner and Bažant, 2013b ) illustrates the composite character of practical models. Its kinematic constraint decomposes strain onto a predefined set of microplane orientations and recovers the macroscopic stress through the principle of virtual work. This component is mechanistic, reflecting a geometric description of how the material transmits stress across orientations. The ‘boundary’ functions that bound the admissible normal and shear stresses on each microplane, however, do not follow from the kinematic constraint. Their functional forms and parameters are selected to reproduce observed uniaxial, biaxial, and triaxial responses. In the terminology used here, these functions provide the phenomenological component of the model. The same pattern recurs in the KCC model ( Malvar et al., 1997 ; Malvar et al., 2000 ; Wu et al., 2012 ; Wu and Crawford, 2015 ) and in LDPM ( Cusatis et al., 2011b ; Cusatis et al., 2011a ) . An explicit structural hypothesis (a pressure-dependent invariant space for KCC, particle geometry and contact kinematics for LDPM) is combined with strength or boundary functions calibrated against experimental data. Hybridization also occurs on the data-driven side. A learned component can be incorporated into a mechanistic model, for example by replacing the microplane boundary functions with a learned surrogate while retaining the kinematic constraint and virtual-work recovery. Alternatively, a learned model can keep the structural skeleton of a phenomenological model (an internal variable, an evolution law, and a stress response) while declining to specify any of them in closed form. Learned models are also routinely constrained to satisfy general mechanical requirements: a convex learned potential yields a hyperelastic, materially stable stress ( As’ad et al., 2022 ) ; invariant inputs enforce frame indifference and material symmetry ( Heider et al., 2020 ; Vlassis et al., 2020 ) ; a sign-constrained evolution enforces irreversibility and nonnegative dissipation ( Masi et al., 2021 ) . Constraints of this kind are not themselves a form of hybridization. Every constitutive model, in all three paradigms, is required to satisfy them. They restrict which relations are admissible, not where a relation originates. In this work, no boundary function is postulated and no return-mapping correction is performed. The stress update itself is learned as a nonparametric map from the current strain and an internal state to the current stress; whatever admissible region the material obeys is therefore implicit in that learned map under physics constraints. What the formulation retains from the models above is their structural skeleton rather than a derivation from any particular mechanism. It is mechanics-informed: the descriptors that drive the state are frame-invariant and the history they accumulate is irreversible. Section 2.4 makes this positioning precise.

sections.heading: 2.2 Constitutive models for quasi-brittle materials
sections.text: Although the method is general, this paper focuses on quasi-brittle materials such as concrete and rock, for which the phenomenological paradigm has long been the dominant approach. Most established constitutive models for concrete and other quasi-brittle materials (including pressure-dependent plasticity ( Drucker and Prager, 1952 ) , cap-plasticity ( DiMaggio and Sandler, 1971 ) , and continuum damage-plasticity formulations ( Lubliner et al., 1989 ) ) share a common predictor-corrector algorithmic structure. At each load increment, a trial stress is first computed elastically from the strain increment and the current elastic stiffness as, 𝝈 t trial = 𝝈 t − 1 + 𝐂 e : Δ ​ 𝜺 t . \bm{\sigma}_{t}^{\mathrm{trial}}=\bm{\sigma}_{t-1}+\mathbf{C}^{e}:\Delta\bm{\varepsilon}_{t}. (1) The trial stress is then tested against an admissible region, which is defined by a scalar yield or failure function, F ⁡ ( 𝝈 , ℋ ) ≤ 0 F(\bm{\sigma},\mathcal{H})\leq 0 , typically written in terms of stress invariants and a set of internal history variables ℋ \mathcal{H} , such as accumulated plastic strain and/or a damage parameter. This function effectively defines a boundary on the elastic domain in stress space. If the trial stress violates the boundary, F ⁡ ( 𝝈 t trial , ℋ t − 1 ) > 0 F(\bm{\sigma}_{t}^{\mathrm{trial}},\mathcal{H}_{t-1})>0 , it is mapped back onto the boundary ( F ⁡ ( 𝝈 , ℋ ) = 0 F(\bm{\sigma},\mathcal{H})=0 ) through a correction step – typically a radial return, closest-point projection, or cutting-plane algorithm – and ℋ \mathcal{H} is updated through an associated or non-associated flow and hardening/damage rule. Because the elastic operator 𝐂 e \mathbf{C}^{e} is prescribed by a small number of elastic constants (even when it is degraded by damage through OPEN ℋ ) \mathcal{H}) and largely independent of material form, essentially all model-specific physics (and the engineering judgment/inference required to calibrate it) is concentrated in the design and evolution of the boundary function F F .

sections.heading: 2.3 A representative example: the KCC model
sections.text: The Karagozian & Case Concrete (KCC) model ( Malvar et al., 1997 ; Malvar et al., 2000 ; Wu et al., 2012 ; Wu and Crawford, 2015 ) is a widely used model for concrete under impact and blast loading that exhibits this phenomenological predictor-corrector structure. KCC first fixes three pressure-dependent reference surfaces in deviatoric stress versus pressure space: a yield surface Δ ​ σ y ​ ( p ) \Delta\sigma_{y}(p) , a maximum (failure) surface Δ ​ σ m ​ ( p ) \Delta\sigma_{m}(p) , and a residual surface Δ ​ σ r ​ ( p ) \Delta\sigma_{r}(p) , where p p denotes the mean pressure. Then the current bounding surface is obtained by interpolating between them as damage accumulates. Each reference surface is specified in closed form as a rational function of the pressure, Δ ​ σ y ​ ( p ) = a 0 ​ y + p a 1 ​ y + a 2 ​ y ​ p , Δ ​ σ m ​ ( p ) = a 0 + p a 1 + a 2 ​ p , Δ ​ σ r ​ ( p ) = p a 1 ​ f + a 2 ​ f ​ p , \Delta\sigma_{y}(p)=a_{0y}+\frac{p}{a_{1y}+a_{2y}p},\qquad\Delta\sigma_{m}(p)=a_{0}+\frac{p}{a_{1}+a_{2}p},\qquad\Delta\sigma_{r}(p)=\frac{p}{a_{1f}+a_{2f}p}, (2) with the constants a 0 ​ y , a 1 ​ y , a 2 ​ y , a 0 , a 1 , a 2 , a 1 ​ f , a 2 ​ f a_{0y},a_{1y},a_{2y},a_{0},a_{1},a_{2},a_{1f},a_{2f} calibrated by curve-fitting unconfined and confined compression and tension test data over the pressure range of interest. A scalar damage-like history variable λ \lambda accumulates with the effective plastic strain increment, and is scaled differently in tension and in compression. A normalized modulation function η ⁡ ( λ ) ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \eta(\lambda)\in[0,1] , which rises from zero to unity as λ \lambda increases to λ m \lambda_{m} and decays back to zero thereafter, interpolates the current strength surface between the yield and maximum surfaces during hardening ( λ ≤ λ m \lambda\leq\lambda_{m} ) and between the maximum and residual surfaces during softening ( λ > λ m \lambda>\lambda_{m} ). The transition value λ m \lambda_{m} is the point at which the current surface coincides with the maximum surface, and corresponds to the peak stress of the stress–strain response, resulting in the pressure and damage dependent surface taking the following form: Δ ​ σ ​ ( p , λ ) = { Δ ​ σ y ​ ( p ) + η ⁡ ( λ ) ​ [ Δ ​ σ m ​ ( p ) − Δ ​ σ y ​ ( p ) ] , λ ≤ λ m , Δ ​ σ r ​ ( p ) + η ⁡ ( λ ) ​ [ Δ ​ σ m ​ ( p ) − Δ ​ σ r ​ ( p ) ] , λ > λ m . \Delta\sigma(p,\lambda)=\begin{cases}\Delta\sigma_{y}(p)+\eta(\lambda)\left[\Delta\sigma_{m}(p)-\Delta\sigma_{y}(p)\right],&\lambda\leq\lambda_{m},\\[4.0pt] \Delta\sigma_{r}(p)+\eta(\lambda)\left[\Delta\sigma_{m}(p)-\Delta\sigma_{r}(p)\right],&\lambda>\lambda_{m}.\end{cases} (3) Here, the value of η \eta itself is supplied as a fitted, often tabulated, function of λ \lambda rather than derived from a constitutive principle. The boundary correction step then scales the trial deviatoric stress radially back onto the current surface Δ ​ σ ​ ( p , λ ) \Delta\sigma(p,\lambda) , preserving the trial stress ratios while the pressure is updated from the volumetric elastic response and λ \lambda is advanced for the next increment. The direction of this correction is set by the flow rule, which in KCC is deviatoric (and hence non-associated with respect to the pressure-dependent surface), with volumetric response supplied by a separate tabulated compaction relation. Strain-rate sensitivity is incorporated through an additional empirical dynamic-increase-factor curve that further rescales the surfaces in Eq. ( 2 ). The elastic-predictor, boundary-correction structure is not confined to single- or multi-surface plasticity models such as KCC. It also underlies constitutive frameworks that depart from a classical yield-surface formulation in stress-invariant space altogether. The microplane model M7 ( Caner and Bažant, 2013a ; Caner and Bažant, 2013b ) formulates the constitutive response on a set of predefined microplanes, planes of differing spatial orientation sampled over a unit hemisphere, rather than directly in terms of stress invariants. On each microplane, normal and shear strain components are related to corresponding stress components through fitted boundary functions that bound the admissible stress as a function of the volumetric, deviatoric, and shear strains on that plane. When the elastically predicted microplane stress vector exceeds its boundary, it is dropped back onto the boundary at constant strain, and the macroscopic stress is recovered from the ensemble of microplane stresses through the principle of virtual work. The admissible-stress region is thus defined plane-by-plane rather than through a single scalar surface, but the same elastic-trial-then-boundary-correction logic applies at the microplane level. A related pattern appears in the Lattice Discrete Particle Model (LDPM) ( Cusatis et al., 2011b ; Cusatis et al., 2011a ) , a meso-scale formulation that represents concrete as an assembly of rigid particles connected through lattice facets rather than as a continuum. At each facet, an elastic law relates the normal and shear strain jumps between particles to facet tractions, and these tractions are in turn bounded by strength domains, for example fracturing, cohesive, and compaction/pore-collapse boundaries, defined as functions of the facet-level stress and strain state and fit to represent tensile, shear, and compressive failure mechanisms and their coupling. As with KCC and the microplane model, the elastic response is evaluated first, and the facet-level state is subsequently mapped back onto a boundary surface designed and calibrated in advance.

sections.heading: 2.4 The phenomenological cost of designing the boundary function
sections.text: Equations ( 2 ) and ( 3 ) exemplify what is implicit in most classical inelastic constitutive models: the elastic predictor in Eq. ( 1 ) is essentially free, but the boundary function that performs the correction must be designed almost entirely from phenomenology. In the case of the KCC model, the three independent pressure-dependent surfaces, a tension/compression-sensitive damage-accumulation rule, a fitted interpolation function η ⁡ ( λ ) \eta(\lambda) , and a separately calibrated rate-dependence curve together require a substantial battery of triaxial, uniaxial, and rate-dependent calibration tests, as well as engineering judgment about the functional forms in Eqs. ( 2 )–( 3 ) themselves and all of the underlying rules. Once fitted, the resulting boundary is tied to the assumed rational and piecewise functional forms, and its predictions away from the calibration database depend on how well those assumed forms extrapolate rather than on a quantity learned directly from data or underlying mechanisms that are known to govern in the extrapolation region. Other constitutive frameworks replace the three KCC surfaces with a cap surface, a Drucker–Prager cone, a continuum damage variable, a set of microplane boundary functions, or lattice-facet strength domains, but the underlying task is the same: the admissible-stress boundary and its history dependence must be explicitly designed, using a chosen functional form and a calibration campaign suited to that form, before the elastic-predictor, boundary-correction update can be used. This difficulty motivates the alternative approach pursued in this paper. Instead of committing in advance to a particular family of pressure-dependent strength surfaces and a fitted damage-interpolation function, the present model lets a latent state and a nonparametric Gaussian-process stress map absorb the analogous role, that of compressing irreversible loading history into quantities that modulate the current stress response directly from observed stress–strain sequences. The boundary-correction logic of Eqs. ( 2 ) and ( 3 ) is not imposed architecturally. Instead, the goal is to test whether a comparable pressure- and history-sensitive constitutive response can be learned through dependence on a small set of latent state variables, without prescribing the surfaces themselves. In the terms of Section 2.1 , this places the present work in the data-driven paradigm. What distinguishes it within that paradigm is how much it deliberately retains from the phenomenological one: a set of internal variables that record loading history, an evolution law driven by a scalar measure of loading progress, and a stress response modulated by the current value of those variables. What it declines to retain is the closed-form specification of each of those ingredients. This approach is developed for broad classes of materials that are rate-independent and path-dependent, as described in Section 4 . It is narrowed to quasi-brittle response only through the specific descriptor and irreversibility choices of Sections 3.4 and 4.2 .

sections.heading: 3.1 Problem statement
sections.text: This section describes the learning problem, specifically defining the internal state variable and the associated evolution law that are inferred from observed stress–strain sequences as well as specifying the information that is assumed to be available for that inference. The observable material response is represented using six-component strain and stress vectors, 𝜺 = [ ε 11 , ε 22 , ε 33 , ε 12 , ε 23 , ε 13 ] ⊤ , 𝝈 = [ σ 11 , σ 22 , σ 33 , σ 12 , σ 23 , σ 13 ] ⊤ . \bm{\varepsilon}=[\varepsilon_{11},\varepsilon_{22},\varepsilon_{33},\varepsilon_{12},\varepsilon_{23},\varepsilon_{13}]^{\top},\qquad\bm{\sigma}=[\sigma_{11},\sigma_{22},\sigma_{33},\sigma_{12},\sigma_{23},\sigma_{13}]^{\top}. (4) Given a collection of stress–strain histories, the goal is to learn an incremental constitutive model of the form 𝝈 t = ℳ ⁡ ( 𝜺 t , ℋ t − 1 ) , \bm{\sigma}_{t}=\mathcal{M}(\bm{\varepsilon}_{t},\mathcal{H}_{t-1}), (5) where ℋ t − 1 \mathcal{H}_{t-1} denotes the unobserved material history accumulated before the current increment. The only information assumed to be available is a finite set of N s N_{s} recorded stress–strain sequences { ( 𝜺 1 : T ( k ) , 𝝈 1 : T ( k ) ) } k = 1 N s \{(\bm{\varepsilon}^{(k)}_{1:T},\bm{\sigma}^{(k)}_{1:T})\}_{k=1}^{N_{s}} , each consisting of T T load increments (the subscript 1 : T 1{:}T denotes increments 1 , … , T 1,\dots,T ), measured at the material-point scale, in which the applied strain path and the resulting stress response are both known at every step. Importantly, the following sources of information are not available : the internal history ℋ \mathcal{H} is never measured directly; no functional form is prescribed for a strength surface, a flow rule, or a hardening law; and no structural-scale force–displacement data are used, so no such form can be back-calculated from structural response. The objective is to learn an incremental model of the form in Eq. ( 5 ) that is usable as a local constitutive update inside a finite element solver. That is, the model must be evaluated independently at each integration point using only information available at that point. Classical constitutive models specify ℋ t − 1 \mathcal{H}_{t-1} through chosen internal variables and evolution laws. In contrast, the present model represents this history through a learned latent state vector 𝒛 t ∈ ℝ d z \bm{z}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}} , 𝝈 t = ℳ ⁡ ( 𝜺 t , 𝒛 t ) , 𝒛 t = 𝒯 ⁡ ( 𝒛 t − 1 , 𝝃 t ) . \bm{\sigma}_{t}=\mathcal{M}(\bm{\varepsilon}_{t},\bm{z}_{t}),\qquad\bm{z}_{t}=\mathcal{T}(\bm{z}_{t-1},\bm{\xi}_{t}). (6) Here 𝝃 t \bm{\xi}_{t} denotes a vector of frame-invariant scalar descriptors of the current increment, formed from the current strain and from the stress state at the end of the previous increment. Its role is to communicate how the material is currently being driven to the evolution law 𝒯 \mathcal{T} , in a form that does not depend on the orientation of the coordinate frame. The set of descriptors that enter 𝝃 t \bm{\xi}_{t} is a material-specific modeling choice and is the one place where knowledge of the material class is used. The choice made for quasi-brittle materials is given in Section 3.4 , and neither the argument of the present section nor the formulation of Section 4 depends on that particular choice. The latent state is not assumed to be a directly measurable physical quantity. It compresses the past loading path into a low-dimensional state needed for the current stress update. This is analogous to the role of internal variables in damage or plasticity theories, but with the representation learned from observable stress–strain sequences. As with classical internal variables, the latent state 𝒛 t \bm{z}_{t} is not uniquely identified by the training data: any invertible reparameterization of 𝒛 t \bm{z}_{t} , absorbed consistently into 𝒯 \mathcal{T} and ℳ \mathcal{M} , reproduces the same stress predictions. The model is therefore identified only up to this functional equivalence class, which is sufficient for the constitutive-update role that 𝒛 t \bm{z}_{t} plays, but also means that individual latent coordinates should not (without further evidence) be assigned a one-to-one physical interpretation such as a specific damage or plastic-strain mechanism. Three questions follow immediately: 1. Why is a memoryless map from 𝜺 t \bm{\varepsilon}_{t} to 𝝈 t \bm{\sigma}_{t} insufficient? 2. To what extent can a learned state vector legitimately replace the full loading path? 3. Can such a latent learned state be interpreted mechanistically? The next two subsections address the first two questions in turn. However, the third question is a more difficult one (as alluded above). It is only addressed anecdotally here, and is left for further investigation in subsequent works that will aim to explore the physical basis of the latent vector and constraints that may be placed on it. In Section 3.4 , the specific choice of 𝝃 t \bm{\xi}_{t} is then specified for the quasi-brittle materials studied here.

sections.heading: 3.2 The use of a latent state
sections.text: A state-space model is a commonly used tool in controls, system identification, and other fields to represents a dynamical system by an internal state that evolves over time and (together with the current input) determines both the next state and the current observation ( Kalman, 1960 ; Särkkä, 2013 ) . The central premise of this representation is that the observation alone is generally not sufficient to predict the future of the system: two systems can share an identical current observation and yet be in different states, and therefore evolve differently from that point onward. Although historically it has not been posed in this way mathematically, the problem of constitutive modeling can be viewed through the state-space formalism. Two material points can be observed at the same instant with an identical current strain 𝜺 t \bm{\varepsilon}_{t} , yet they may have accumulated different histories of damage, plastic strain, or micro-cracking at the micro-, meso-, or macroscale, over the loading paths that produced that strain. These internal quantities are not directly measurable in a standard stress–strain test, yet they are critical to understanding the evolution of the material with deformation. A constitutive law therefore cannot be a memoryless map from strain to stress. Of course this is well-understood in the materials modeling field. The distinction here is that classical constitutive theories supply this representation explicitly, through prescribed damage or plastic-strain variables. The state-space formulation pursued in this work instead treats it as an implicit state to be learned.

sections.heading: 3.3 Markov structure and probabilistic factorization
sections.text: The state-space formulation of Eq. ( 6 ) is only meaningful if the constitutive update can be made Markovian in some state. That is, there must exist a (possibly high-dimensional) history summary ℋ t \mathcal{H}_{t} such that, conditioned on ℋ t \mathcal{H}_{t} , the future stress response is independent of the specific strain–stress path that produced ℋ t \mathcal{H}_{t} . Probabilistically, this is stated as follows. Let π ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \pi(\cdot) and π ( ⋅ ∣ ⋅ ) \pi(\cdot\mid\cdot) denote joint probability and conditional probability densities, and 𝒛 ∼ π ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \bm{z}\sim\pi(\cdot) means that 𝒛 \bm{z} is distributed according to that density. The Markov property states that: π ( 𝝈 t + 1 : T ∣ 𝜺 1 : T , 𝝈 1 : t , ℋ t ) = π ( 𝝈 t + 1 : T ∣ 𝜺 t + 1 : T , ℋ t ) . \pi\!\left(\bm{\sigma}_{t+1:T}\mid\bm{\varepsilon}_{1:T},\bm{\sigma}_{1:t},\mathcal{H}_{t}\right)=\pi\!\left(\bm{\sigma}_{t+1:T}\mid\bm{\varepsilon}_{t+1:T},\mathcal{H}_{t}\right). (7) This is the same assumption that classical internal-variable constitutive theories make. Damage, plastic strain, and hardening variables are constructed so that the current stress increment can be computed from the current strain increment and the current values of these variables, without re-examining the entire loading history. It is also the assumption that underlies the Kalman filter and its nonlinear, Gaussian-process extensions ( Kalman, 1960 ; Wang et al., 2008 ; Krishnan et al., 2017 ) . Replacing the full path with a state is only valid and useful if that state is Markovian. Here, the learned latent state 𝒛 t \bm{z}_{t} is constructed to satisfy Eq. ( 7 ) by design, since Eq. ( 6 ) defines 𝒛 t \bm{z}_{t} recursively from 𝒛 t − 1 \bm{z}_{t-1} and the current-step descriptors 𝝃 t \bm{\xi}_{t} , and never from the strain–stress history directly. It follows that 𝒛 t \bm{z}_{t} is Markovian by construction rather than by empirical verification, and its adequacy as a finite-dimensional summary of ℋ t \mathcal{H}_{t} is tested in the verification cases of Section 6 . This Markov structure also makes the finite element deployment of Section 5 practical. Because 𝒛 t \bm{z}_{t} (together with the previous-step stress from which 𝝃 t \bm{\xi}_{t} is formed) is sufficient to continue the update, it can be stored as a small, fixed-size solver state variable at each integration point, rather than requiring the full strain history to be retained and replayed at every increment. Given this Markov state, the model factorizes into a transition step, which governs the evolution of the latent step, and an observation step, which specifies the conditional distribution of 𝝈 t \bm{\sigma}_{t} given the current state: 𝒛 t ∼ π ⁡ ( 𝒛 t ∣ 𝒛 t − 1 , 𝝃 t ) , 𝝈 t ∼ π ⁡ ( 𝝈 t ∣ 𝒛 t , 𝜺 t ) . \bm{z}_{t}\sim\pi(\bm{z}_{t}\mid\bm{z}_{t-1},\bm{\xi}_{t}),\qquad\bm{\sigma}_{t}\sim\pi(\bm{\sigma}_{t}\mid\bm{z}_{t},\bm{\varepsilon}_{t}). (8) The nominal transition used for inference and finite element deployment is deterministic given the descriptors, 𝒛 t = 𝒯 ⁡ ( 𝒛 t − 1 , 𝝃 t ) \bm{z}_{t}=\mathcal{T}(\bm{z}_{t-1},\bm{\xi}_{t}) as in Eq. ( 6 ). During training, increment-scaled Gaussian perturbations are added to this transition and marginalized by Monte Carlo rollout, as detailed in Section 4 . This regularizes the learned state trajectory but is not propagated in the deployed constitutive update. Only the Gaussian-process stress map requires an inducing-point posterior approximation, in which a small set of representative points summarizes the training data so that the cost of evaluating the stress map does not grow with the number of observations. The model therefore does not, in its present form, quantify epistemic uncertainty in the learned history representation itself, only uncertainty in the stress prediction conditioned on that history. The transition parameters are point estimates, and the state noise introduced during training is a fixed learned quantity rather than a posterior.

The model becomes material specific when we choose the scalar descriptors that make up 𝝃 t \bm{\xi}_{t} and drive the latent transition. The choices made below specialize the general setting to isotropic quasi-brittle materials under triaxial loading, where pressure sensitivity and deviatoric stress intensity are the dominant drivers of the inelastic response. These descriptors do not replace the full tensorial stress–strain relation. Instead, they provide compact mechanics-informed inputs for latent-state evolution. The choice of I 1 I_{1} and J 2 J_{2} is not arbitrary. Rather, it mirrors the pressure–deviatoric split that underlies the boundary functions of Section 2 . The mean stress p = I 1 / 3 p=I_{1}/3 controls confinement-dependent strength and stiffness in exactly the way the yield, maximum, and residual surfaces Δ ​ σ y ​ ( p ) \Delta\sigma_{y}(p) , Δ ​ σ m ​ ( p ) \Delta\sigma_{m}(p) , Δ ​ σ r ​ ( p ) \Delta\sigma_{r}(p) of Eq. ( 2 ) are parameterized by pressure, while 3 ​ J 2 \sqrt{3J_{2}} , a von-Mises equivalent stress, measures the distortional stress intensity that drives shear-dominated microcracking and is the quantity actually compared against those surfaces. Feeding I 1 I_{1} and J 2 J_{2} into the latent transition therefore gives the learned history variable access to the same two stress descriptors that a classical pressure-dependent plasticity model would use to evaluate its yield function, without committing to the specific rational functional forms of e.g. Eqs. ( 2 )–( 3 ). The equivalent strain ε eq \varepsilon^{\mathrm{eq}} of Eq. ( 9 ) is an explicit state variable. It is an accumulating scalar measures of loading progression used to drive history evolution, that is used in lieu of the full strain tensor. Together with the state vector 𝒛 t \bm{z}_{t} , it plays a role analogous to the the scalar damage-like history variable λ \lambda of Eq. ( 3 ). Unlike λ \lambda , which evolves through a pressure dependent function h ⁡ ( p ) h(p) acting on the evolution of effective plastic strain as λ ˙ = h ⁡ ( p ) ​ ε ¯ ˙ p \dot{\lambda}=h(p)\dot{\bar{\varepsilon}}^{p} (14) where ε ¯ ˙ p = 2 / 3 ​ 𝜺 ˙ p : 𝜺 ˙ p \dot{\bar{\varepsilon}}^{p}=\sqrt{2/3\dot{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{p}:\dot{\bm{\varepsilon}}^{p}} and h ⁡ ( p ) h(p) requires calibration, ε eq \varepsilon^{\mathrm{eq}} is defined directly from the strain tensor and it deliberately excludes the volumetric strain component. For quasi-brittle materials under triaxial compression, volumetric and deviatoric strain are governed by different mechanisms: volumetric strain reflects competing pore collapse and microcrack dilatancy, whereas deviatoric strain grows steadily through frictional sliding and crack growth. The pressure channel through which volumetric information enters the model is instead carried by the stress invariant I 1 I_{1} , consistent with the classical treatment in stress-space rather than a strain-space quantity. During supervised training, previous-step invariants may be computed from measured stresses to stabilize the latent rollout and expose the transition to physically meaningful pressure and deviatoric descriptors. During finite element deployment, measured stresses are unavailable and the same invariants are recomputed from the model-predicted stress at the previous increment. The deployed update is therefore fully local and self-contained. Violating frame invariance is a recognized failure mode of neural-network constitutive models. Without architectural or data-level safeguards, such models can learn spurious dependence on the arbitrary orientation of the material coordinate frame, so that the predicted stress changes when the same deformation is merely expressed in a rotated frame ( Heider et al., 2020 ; Vlassis et al., 2020 ) . The present model addresses this concern in two complementary ways. First, the latent transition depends only on the rotation-invariant descriptors ε eq \varepsilon^{\mathrm{eq}} , I 1 I_{1} , and J 2 J_{2} . Second, the Gaussian-process stress map is trained under SO(3) rotational data augmentation (Section 5 ).

sections.heading: 4 Gaussian-process state-space constitutive formulation
sections.text: As one instance of this structure, the implementation developed here evolves the latent variable with a deterministic neural map and predicts stress with a Gaussian process, so as to balance speed with the need for uncertainty quantification. The transition is evaluated at every integration point at every increment and is kept cheap, while the stress map retains a posterior variance that provides an epistemic measure for where the training data do and do not constrain the prediction.

sections.heading: 4.1 Latent state evolution
sections.text: The constitutive model is written as a discrete state-space model, 𝝈 t = g ⁡ ( 𝒛 t , 𝜺 t ) + 𝐯 t , 𝒛 t = 𝒛 t − 1 + Δ ​ 𝒛 t , \bm{\sigma}_{t}=g(\bm{z}_{t},\bm{\varepsilon}_{t})+\mathbf{v}_{t},\qquad\bm{z}_{t}=\bm{z}_{t-1}+\Delta\bm{z}_{t}, (15) where g g is a probabilistic stress map and 𝐯 t \mathbf{v}_{t} is a discrepancy (or noise) term. The latent-state increment, Δ ​ 𝒛 t \Delta\bm{z}_{t} , is parameterized by a neural transition function of the latent state together with two ingredients that describe how the material is being driven. The first is a scalar loading-progress parameter κ \kappa , which measures the increment of deformation applied in a given step. The second is the frame-invariant descriptor vector 𝝃 t \bm{\xi}_{t} introduced in Section 3 , which summarizes the conditions under which the current increment is applied. The transition is then modeled by Δ ​ 𝒛 t = f θ ​ [ 𝒛 t − 1 , 𝝃 t ] ​ | Δ ​ κ ~ t | , \Delta\bm{z}_{t}=f_{\theta}\left[\bm{z}_{t-1},\bm{\xi}_{t}\right]\left|\Delta\tilde{\kappa}_{t}\right|, (16) where tildes denote normalized quantities and Δ ​ κ ~ t = κ t − κ t − 1 s κ , \Delta\tilde{\kappa}_{t}=\frac{\kappa_{t}-\kappa_{t-1}}{s_{\kappa}}, (17) with s κ s_{\kappa} a fixed scale constant. Note the similarity between the discrete form in Eq. ( 16 ) and the continuous damage evolution law in Eq. ( 14 ). However, while Eq. ( 14 ) is strongly prescriptive, the proposed state transition function is general and highly flexible. Indeed, the progress parameter κ \kappa , the descriptor vector 𝝃 \bm{\xi} , the dimension of the state vector 𝒛 t \bm{z}_{t} , and any constraint placed on the output of f θ f_{\theta} are not specified here. They are material-dependent and can be customized to account for the specific mechanisms, constraints, and data available for a given material. For quasi-brittle materials, these are assigned in Section 4.2 . The rate-times-increment form in Eq. ( 16 ) encodes the central inductive bias of the formulation. That is, the neural network learns a rate of latent variable evolution per unit of deformation, not an increment. Because the update is scaled by | Δ ​ κ ~ t | |\Delta\tilde{\kappa}_{t}| , the latent state advances only when deformation progresses, and when the increment in κ \kappa is nearly zero the same factor suppresses artificial latent drift. Nothing in Eq. ( 16 ) restricts the sign of that rate, so a history variable that can decrease is admissible. Instead, material-specific knowledge about which evolutions are admissible is injected by constraining the output of f θ f_{\theta} , and Section 4.2 does exactly that for the material class studied here. Eq. ( 16 ) is a general form, but it is not a universal one. First, it assumes rate independence . Evolution is parameterized by κ \kappa rather than by time, so two loadings that trace the same path at different speeds produce the same response. A rate-dependent material, whether through viscoplasticity or through strain-rate-sensitive strength, would require replacing κ \kappa by a time-parameterized deformation measure, at the cost of the sampling-rate invariance described next. Second, it assumes that 𝝃 t \bm{\xi}_{t} is frame invariant . If any component of 𝝃 t \bm{\xi}_{t} changes under a rigid rotation of the coordinate frame, so would the predicted latent evolution, and the constitutive update would inherit a dependence on an arbitrary choice of material axes. Together these two assumptions restrict the present formulation to rate-independent, path-dependent materials. Within that class, the remaining physics enters through the choice of κ \kappa , 𝝃 \bm{\xi} , the dimension of 𝒛 t \bm{z}_{t} , and the constraints placed on f θ f_{\theta} . It is at this level, not in Eq. ( 16 ) itself, that our approach commits to a particular material class. The rate-times-increment factorization also decouples the learned state-evolution tendency from the sampling interval of the training data. The network f θ f_{\theta} predicts a rate per unit of loading progress, while | Δ ​ κ ~ t | |\Delta\tilde{\kappa}_{t}| rescales that rate to the increment actually observed, so the same trained transition remains valid whether a loading path is sampled finely or coarsely. This is particularly useful for finite element deployment, where the solver increment is set by explicit stability and mesh constraints rather than by the experimental sampling interval, yet requires no retraining of the transition to accommodate. Writing the update in the continuum limit of small increments gives an ordinary differential equation in deformation progress rather than in real time, d ​ 𝒛 d ​ κ = f θ ​ [ 𝒛 , 𝝃 ] ​ sign ⁡ ( Δ ​ κ ) , \frac{d\bm{z}}{d\kappa}=f_{\theta}\left[\bm{z},\bm{\xi}\right]\operatorname{sign}(\Delta\kappa), (18) which makes explicit that the latent evolution is parameterized by κ \kappa rather than by wall-clock or explicit-solver time.

sections.heading: 4.2 Specialization to quasi-brittle materials
sections.text: For the isotropic and rate-independent quasi-brittle materials studied here, the material-dependent ingredients of Eq. ( 16 ) are assigned as κ = ε eq , 𝝃 t = ( ε ~ t eq , I ~ 1 , t − 1 , J ~ 2 , t − 1 ) , f θ ≥ 𝟎 , \kappa=\varepsilon^{\mathrm{eq}},\qquad\bm{\xi}_{t}=\left(\tilde{\varepsilon}^{\mathrm{eq}}_{t},\tilde{I}_{1,t-1},\tilde{J}_{2,t-1}\right),\qquad f_{\theta}\geq\mathbf{0}, (19) with ε eq \varepsilon^{\mathrm{eq}} the equivalent strain of Eq. ( 9 ) and I 1 I_{1} , J 2 J_{2} are the stress invariants of Section 3.4 , each entering the network in its normalized form. Equivalent strain is a natural loading-progress parameter for this material class because the quasi-static triaxial data used for training are rate independent, so deformation rather than time is the meaningful measure of how far a loading path has advanced. The nonnegativity of f θ f_{\theta} is imposed through a softplus output nonlinearity, and it represents the material-specific inductive bias of the present application. It makes Δ ​ 𝒛 t ≥ 𝟎 \Delta\bm{z}_{t}\geq\mathbf{0} at every increment and, in the continuum limit of Eq. ( 18 ), it makes d ​ 𝒛 / d ​ κ ≥ 𝟎 d\bm{z}/d\kappa\geq\mathbf{0} as loading progresses, so the latent state accumulates along a loading path and never reverses. This is appropriate here because the mechanisms the latent state stands in for, namely damage, compaction, and microcrack growth, only accumulate. This assumption would not be appropriate for a material whose history variable must be able to decrease, such as kinematic hardening and the associated Bauschinger effect, or porosity. Eq. ( 16 ) admits such materials; only the sign constraint imposed here excludes them. In the present implementation, the transition network is a multilayer perceptron with input dimension five and output dimension d z = 2 d_{z}=2 . It uses three hidden layers of width 64 with hyperbolic-tangent activations, followed by the softplus output nonlinearity. The scalar descriptors ε eq \varepsilon^{\mathrm{eq}} , I 1 I_{1} , and J 2 J_{2} are invariant under rigid coordinate rotations, so the state-transition rate is not tied to a particular material-axis orientation. Mechanically, Eq. ( 16 ) plays the role that a flow rule and hardening law play in classical rate-independent plasticity. The plastic multiplier is replaced by the equivalent-strain increment | Δ ​ ε ~ t eq | |\Delta\tilde{\varepsilon}^{\mathrm{eq}}_{t}| , and the flow direction and magnitude are replaced by the learned, invariant-dependent nonnegative rate f θ ​ [ ⋅ ] f_{\theta}[\cdot] . The hyperbolic-tangent hidden-layer activations keep f θ f_{\theta} smooth and bounded, which in turn keeps the right-hand side of Eq. ( 18 ) Lipschitz in 𝒛 \bm{z} . This is a modeling choice rather than an enforced constraint, but it favors a well-behaved, non-stiff latent trajectory when Eq. ( 16 ) is integrated explicitly at the small time increments used by the explicit finite element solver.

(20) Feeding a jointly trained representation into a Gaussian-process kernel in this way follows the deep-kernel-learning precedent, in which a neural network produces the feature space over which a GP operates ( Wilson et al., 2016 ) . The difference is that 𝒛 t \bm{z}_{t} here is not a fixed embedding of a single input but a recurrent latent state that retains information about preceding loading increments. Each stress component is modeled by a Gaussian process with a radial basis function (RBF) kernel and automatic relevance determination (ARD), k a ( 𝒙 , 𝒙 ′ ) = α a 2 exp [ − 1 2 ∑ r = 1 d z + 6 ( x r − x r ′ ) 2 ℓ a , r 2 ] , a = 1 , … , 6 . k_{a}(\bm{x},\bm{x}^{\prime})=\alpha_{a}^{2}\exp\left[-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{r=1}^{d_{z}+6}\frac{(x_{r}-x_{r}^{\prime})^{2}}{\ell_{a,r}^{2}}\right],\qquad a=1,\ldots,6. (21) The ARD length scales ℓ a , r \ell_{a,r} give each output its own sensitivity to every latent-state and strain coordinate. Small ℓ a , r \ell_{a,r} implies rapid variation of stress component a a along input direction r r , while large ℓ a , r \ell_{a,r} implies weak dependence over the range represented by the data. The six latent GPs have separate means, kernels, and variational distributions and are conditionally independent given 𝒙 t \bm{x}_{t} . They remain coupled through their common dependence on the latent history 𝒛 t \bm{z}_{t} and current strain 𝜺 t \bm{\varepsilon}_{t} , but the output layer contains no explicit cross-output covariance or coregionalization kernel ( Álvarez et al., 2012 ) . This choice keeps the six posterior-mean evaluations independent at deployment, at the cost of not representing residual cross-component covariance beyond the dependence already expressed by 𝒙 t \bm{x}_{t} . Exact GP regression with a Gaussian likelihood has a closed-form posterior, but factorizing the covariance matrix over N N training points requires 𝒪 ⁡ ( N 3 ) \mathcal{O}(N^{3}) operations and 𝒪 ⁡ ( N 2 ) \mathcal{O}(N^{2}) storage. sections.heading: 4.4 Role of uncertainty
sections.text: The GP observation model defines both a posterior mean and a posterior variance. This is important because limited triaxial data (which is what we use in the training) cannot cover all loading paths that may arise in a finite element analysis. The probabilistic structure can therefore be used offline to identify data-sparse regions, compare model variants, facilitate uncertainty propagation, and guide active learning. This is a direct statistical countermeasure to the phenomenological limitation identified in Section 2 . For example, the rational functions of Eq. ( 2 ) extrapolate according to a fixed, assumed functional form and cannot signal when a prediction has left the calibration regime, whereas the GP posterior variance grows, in principle, in regions of the joint latent-state/strain space that are far from the inducing points and training data. This provides an inbuilt, quantitative indicator of interpolation/extrapolation risk rather than relying on engineering judgment about functional-form validity. The GP can also account for noise or inherent stochastic variability in the material behavior and the associated training data. In fact, the probabilistic structure retained by the sparse variational formulation allows this predicted stress uncertainty to be separated into contributions of distinct origin. Because the latent state enters the stress map as a random variable, the predictive variance follows from the law of total variance, Var [ 𝝈 t ∣ 𝜺 1 : t ] ⏟ total = 𝔼 𝐳 t ​ [ Var GP ⁡ ( 𝝈 t ∣ 𝐳 t , 𝜺 t ) ] ⏟ σ GP 2 + Var 𝐳 t ⁡ [ 𝔼 GP ​ ( 𝝈 t ∣ 𝐳 t , 𝜺 t ) ] ⏟ σ 𝐳 2 + σ n 2 ⏟ likelihood , \underbrace{\operatorname{Var}\!\left[\bm{\sigma}_{t}\mid\bm{\varepsilon}_{1:t}\right]}_{\text{total}}=\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}_{t}}\!\left[\operatorname{Var}_{\mathrm{GP}}\!\left(\bm{\sigma}_{t}\mid\mathbf{z}_{t},\bm{\varepsilon}_{t}\right)\right]}_{\displaystyle\sigma^{2}_{\mathrm{GP}}}+\underbrace{\operatorname{Var}_{\mathbf{z}_{t}}\!\left[\mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{GP}}\!\left(\bm{\sigma}_{t}\mid\mathbf{z}_{t},\bm{\varepsilon}_{t}\right)\right]}_{\displaystyle\sigma^{2}_{\mathbf{z}}}+\underbrace{\sigma^{2}_{n}}_{\text{likelihood}}, (32) evaluated component-wise on the six stress components, where the first term denotes the epistemic variance of the stress prediction, the second term relates to the aleatory stochasticity in the latent state evolution, and the final term is a stochastic noise. In the implementation, the outer expectation is taken over S eval = 100 S_{\mathrm{eval}}=100 Monte Carlo rollouts of the latent trajectory, each propagated from 𝐳 0 = 𝟎 \mathbf{z}_{0}=\mathbf{0} through the stochastic transition of Eq. ( 27 ), with the sparse GP posterior evaluated along every realisation. This is deliberately larger than the S = 3 S=3 samples used during training when evaluating the loss of Eq. ( 28 ). During training, the average only has to supply an unbiased gradient, whereas the variance decomposition reported during model evaluation requires a converged estimate of each individual term. The three terms have distinct physical interpretations. The epistemic term, σ GP 2 \sigma^{2}_{\mathrm{GP}} , is the posterior variance of the sparse GP at the query point ( 𝐳 t , 𝜺 t ) (\mathbf{z}_{t},\bm{\varepsilon}_{t}) , averaged over the sampled latent trajectories. It measures how far the current state–strain pair lies from the inducing-point support built during training, and therefore reports the degree to which the model is extrapolating. It is the only term that is reducible by performing additional experiments. Collecting a new loading history that covers a previously unseen region of state–strain space reduces this term. The remaining two terms, by contrast, cannot be reduced by adding data. The latent-induced term, σ 𝐳 2 \sigma^{2}_{\mathbf{z}} , arises because the transition network carries a learnable state noise, the increment-scaled perturbation σ z ​ | Δ ​ ε ~ t eq | ​ 𝐰 t ( s ) \sigma_{z}|\Delta\tilde{\varepsilon}^{\mathrm{eq}}_{t}|\mathbf{w}_{t}^{(s)} of Eq. ( 27 ), so that different rollouts reach slightly different states at the same strain. It is the resulting spread of the GP posterior mean due to randomness in the latent state, and quantifies how strongly the stress prediction is influenced by uncertainty in the inferred history variable. It will grow, for example, if the learned state provides a highly variable summary of the latent history, which might occur when the stress-strain response of the material is highly variable under nominally identical conditions. The aleatoric term σ n 2 \sigma^{2}_{n} is the learned homoscedastic noise of the multitask Gaussian likelihood, and is constant along a sequence and across sequences. All three are computed in the normalized stress units used for training and recovered in physical units through the scaling in Eq. ( 31 ). Since the aleatoric terms are essentially the same for every sequence, they do not change how sequences compare. That is, ranking candidate experiments by the total predictive standard deviation or by the epistemic term alone gives the same order. Reporting the split, rather than the total alone makes the distinction available to the user for actions such as active learning. A fixed-form constitutive model calibrated by least squares supplies a single parameter set and no comparable internal measure of where its calibration is unsupported. In the present VUMAT implementation, only the posterior mean in Eq. ( 29 ) is evaluated for efficiency and robustness. Thus, the finite element results reported below should be interpreted as posterior-mean deployment results, not as a full uncertainty-propagating finite element analysis – which the proposed framework enables but are left for future work.

sections.heading: 4.5 Framework overview
sections.text: Figure 1 summarizes the incremental constitutive update. At each time step t t , the current strain 𝜺 t \bm{\varepsilon}_{t} is used to calculate the equivalent strain and its increment. Together with the previous latent state 𝒛 t − 1 \bm{z}_{t-1} and the previous-step stress invariants I 1 , t − 1 I_{1,t-1} and J 2 , t − 1 J_{2,t-1} , these inputs determine the latent evolution rate through a multilayer perceptron. A softplus transformation makes the deterministic rate nonnegative, and multiplication by the magnitude of the normalized equivalent-strain increment gives the latent-state increment in Eq. ( 16 ). The updated state 𝒛 t \bm{z}_{t} is then combined with the current strain and passed to the sparse GP stress map to predict the six stress components. The terms 𝐰 t \mathbf{w}_{t} and 𝐯 t \mathbf{v}_{t} in the schematic represent latent-transition and observation noise, respectively; the implemented transition noise is scaled by the equivalent-strain increment as in Eq. ( 27 ). During closed-loop prediction, the predicted stress supplies the invariants for the next step, while 𝒛 t \bm{z}_{t} carries the accumulated loading history forward. The transition network and GP stress map are trained jointly, whereas finite element deployment evaluates the deterministic latent update and GP posterior mean. ( 16 ) to obtain 𝒛 t \bm{z}_{t} , which together with the current strain 𝜺 t \bm{\varepsilon}_{t} is mapped by the Gaussian-process stress map g g to the stress 𝝈 t \bm{\sigma}_{t} .

sections.heading: 5.1 Stress–strain histories and normalization
sections.text: Training begins by providing a set of N hist N_{\text{hist}} triaxial stress-strain histories separated into an N train / N val / N test N_{\text{train}}/N_{\text{val}}/N_{\text{test}} training/validation/test sequences, with the exact counts used in this study provided in A . Each sequence is preprocessed by removing the initial transient segment, inserting a zero reference state, truncating by equivalent strain, and normalizing strain, stress, equivalent strain, I 1 I_{1} , and J 2 J_{2} . The zero reference state gives the recurrent model a common undeformed initial condition, while equivalent-strain truncation prevents the training objective from being dominated by extreme extrapolation regions outside the intended calibration domain. The normalization convention for a quantity ξ \xi is given by ξ ~ = ξ − μ ξ s ξ . \tilde{\xi}=\frac{\xi-\mu_{\xi}}{s_{\xi}}. (33) A shared scalar standard deviation is used for all six strain components, and another shared scalar standard deviation is used for all six stress components, rather than normalizing each component independently. This choice is important for rotational augmentation. Because the original triaxial data contain nearly zero shear components, component-wise normalization would artificially amplify rotated shear components. Shared tensor-component scaling instead preserves the relative structure of the stress and strain tensors under rotation. The scalar descriptors ε eq \varepsilon^{\mathrm{eq}} , I 1 I_{1} , and J 2 J_{2} are normalized independently, since they are already rotation-invariant scalars and do not share this constraint. The specific normalization statistics fitted for the exported model used in the present verification are reported in B .

sections.heading: 5.2 Temporal downsampling
sections.text: Because the model is trained directly on experimentally measurable quantities (the stress and strain histories themselves, rather than on a quantity defined at a fixed clock rate), it must also accommodate the fact that different triaxial tests, and different finite element solves, are not recorded or advanced at a common temporal resolution. One experiment may report tens of points along a loading path, another many thousands, and neither sampling rate is dictated by the material response itself. A constitutive model that learned a rate with respect to wall-clock or step time would inherit this arbitrary choice of sampling protocol as if it were physical information. The latent transition of Eq. ( 16 ) avoids this by construction. What the network f θ f_{\theta} learns is not an increment but a rate, d ​ 𝒛 / d ​ ε eq d\bm{z}/d\varepsilon^{\mathrm{eq}}{} in the continuum limit of Eq. ( 18 ) with κ = ε eq \kappa=\varepsilon^{\mathrm{eq}} , defined with respect to equivalent-strain progression rather than time. The actual size of the latent-state update at a given step is then obtained only afterward, by multiplying this rate by the measured equivalent-strain increment | Δ ​ ε ~ t eq | |\Delta\tilde{\varepsilon}^{\mathrm{eq}}_{t}| between consecutive observations. Two recordings of the same physical loading path sampled at different densities therefore differ only in how many times the same underlying rate law is queried and integrated, not in the rate law itself, so the learned constitutive response is time-resolution-independent and can be built purely from heterogeneous, unevenly sampled experimental observations without first resampling them onto a common time base. This rate-based construction further justifies a temporal downsampling to reduce data demands during training. Since the transition model already treats sampling density as a numerical, not a physical, degree of freedom, reducing the number of retained points along a trajectory only coarsens the numerical integration of Eq. ( 18 ) without altering the underlying rate being learned. A full-resolution triaxial history typically has more time steps than the recurrent latent-state model needs, particularly along the post-peak plateau, where stress stays nearly constant over a long strain range. Each sequence is therefore subsampled along its loading axis to a fixed number of points, after the post-peak plateau truncation and normalization-statistics computation of Section 5.1 have already been applied to the full-resolution data. A curvature-based scheme that concentrates points near the pre-peak rise and peak could prioritize coverage of the mechanically decisive regions. However, this work uses the simpler alternative of evenly spaced indices along the truncated sequence, which retains the pre-peak rise, peak, and post-peak plateau in the same proportion as the original record. Every per-time-step channel (strain, stress, equivalent strain, and the invariants I 1 I_{1} and J 2 J_{2} together with their lagged counterparts) is indexed identically, preserving temporal alignment across channels exactly. Figure 2 shows that the retained points track the full-resolution curve through the elastic branch, peak, and residual plateau without visible loss of resolution. Two downsampling targets are used during optimization, reflecting the different roles of the training and validation calculations. Training sequences, and the corresponding non-autoregressive evaluation, are reduced to N tpts = 100 N_{\mathrm{tpts}}=100 points per sequence, while the more computationally expensive autoregressive validation rollout used for checkpoint selection is evaluated on N vpts = 500 N_{\mathrm{vpts}}=500 points per sequence. This optimization-time validation is distinct from the final offline evaluation in Section 6.1 where, after checkpoint selection, both validation and test sequences are evaluated over their complete preprocessed time histories, without temporal downsampling. Downsampling is performed once during dataset construction rather than being redrawn at each training epoch, so that all epochs train on the same fixed set of points per sequence.
