Black lines denote the full-resolution sequence after plateau truncation; red markers denote the N tpts = 100 N_{\mathrm{tpts}}=100 points retained by evenly spaced index selection. The elastic branch, peak, and post-peak plateau are all preserved in the reduced sequence.

sections.heading: 5.3 Rotational augmentation
sections.text: Here the material is treated as isotropic at the scale of the representative volume element (RVE), so that the constitutive response depends on the current strain state and loading history alone, not on the orientation of that strain state relative to any fixed material texture. This is consistent with classical continuum and microplane treatments of plain concrete and related quasi-brittle materials, which idealize the initial material state as statistically isotropic and introduce no prescribed material texture or preferred orientation ( Bažant and Oh, 1985 ; Bažant and Planas, 1998 ; Lubliner et al., 1989 ) . The assumption matters in practice because the available triaxial histories are all recorded in a single laboratory frame, with the axial loading direction aligned to a fixed coordinate axis, while a finite element mesh built from this model (in particular the multi-element structural model) presents strain states at whatever orientation the local element axes happen to have relative to that frame. A stress map trained only on axis-aligned data has no guarantee of behaving consistently once queried far from that orientation, because frame invariance is not automatically guaranteed in neural-network constitutive models and must be enforced through suitable inputs, architectures, loss functions, or data augmentation ( Heider et al., 2020 ; Vlassis et al., 2020 ) . Under RVE-scale isotropy, the constitutive law must satisfy the classical frame-indifference condition ( Truesdell and Noll, 2004 ) . For a proper rotation 𝐑 ∈ SO ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathbf{R}\in\mathrm{SO}(3) , strain and stress tensors transform as 𝜺 ′ = 𝐑 ​ 𝜺 ​ 𝐑 ⊤ \bm{\varepsilon}^{\prime}=\mathbf{R}\bm{\varepsilon}\mathbf{R}^{\top} and 𝝈 ′ = 𝐑 ​ 𝝈 ​ 𝐑 ⊤ \bm{\sigma}^{\prime}=\mathbf{R}\bm{\sigma}\mathbf{R}^{\top} , and the stress map must satisfy the equivariance condition g ⁡ ( 𝐑 ​ 𝜺 ​ 𝐑 ⊤ , ⋅ ) = 𝐑 ​ g ​ ( 𝜺 , ⋅ ) ​ 𝐑 ⊤ g(\mathbf{R}\bm{\varepsilon}\mathbf{R}^{\top},\cdot)=\mathbf{R}\,g(\bm{\varepsilon},\cdot)\,\mathbf{R}^{\top} for every 𝐑 \mathbf{R} . The sparse GP of Section 4 is a generic nonparametric regressor with no architectural mechanism that enforces this condition exactly, unlike equivariant network constructions built specifically for this purpose ( Heider et al., 2020 ; Vlassis et al., 2020 ) . Rotational augmentation instead aims to satisfy this constraint in an approximate, statistical form. By training on many rotated copies of the same physical loading history, the model is encouraged to interpolate consistently across orientations that its architecture does not constrain directly. Concretely, a fixed set of N R = 20 N_{R}=20 rotations is constructed once and applied to every retained stress–strain history. For each history, the same 𝐑 \mathbf{R} is applied to every strain and stress tensor pair ( 𝜺 t , 𝝈 t ) (\bm{\varepsilon}_{t},\bm{\sigma}_{t}) along a given history. The set is a deterministic quasi-uniform covering of SO ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SO}(3) rather than a finite random sample. Five axes are placed on S 2 S^{2} by the golden-angle construction, and each axis is combined with four equally spaced in-plane rotations about it, giving 5 × 4 = 20 5\times 4=20 orientations. It is essential that 𝐑 \mathbf{R} be held fixed along a given trajectory rather than resampled at each time step. A time-varying rotation would not correspond to a change of orientation at all, but would superimpose a spurious, time-varying rigid rotation on top of the physical deformation, corrupting the sequential structure from which the latent transition of Section 4 is meant to learn. The N R = 20 N_{R}=20 rotated copies of each sequence are added to the training set only. Validation and test sequences, and the normalization statistics of Section 5.1 , are computed from unrotated data, so that checkpoint selection and all reported errors are measured on physically distinct loading histories rather than on rotations of sequences the model has already seen. The training set therefore comprises N train × ( 1 + 20 ) N_{\text{train}}\times(1+20) sequences, and the six-component GP stress map is exposed to many orientations of the same underlying material response. The latent transition and the stress map require different treatments under rotation. The transition updates the latent state using only the scalar descriptors ε eq \varepsilon^{\mathrm{eq}} , I 1 I_{1} , and J 2 J_{2} , all of which are unchanged when the strain and stress tensors are rotated by 𝐑 \mathbf{R} . Consequently, rotating an entire loading history leaves the inputs to the transition unchanged and produces the same latent-state trajectory. That is, rotational augmentation adds no new information to this part of the model. The stress map g g , by contrast, receives the components of the strain tensor and returns the components of the stress tensor. It must therefore satisfy the equivariance relation g ⁡ ( 𝐑 ​ 𝜺 ​ 𝐑 ⊤ , 𝒛 ) = 𝐑 ​ g ​ ( 𝜺 , 𝒛 ) ​ 𝐑 ⊤ , g(\mathbf{R}\bm{\varepsilon}\mathbf{R}^{\top},\bm{z})=\mathbf{R}\,g(\bm{\varepsilon},\bm{z})\,\mathbf{R}^{\top}, (34) which is not enforced by the generic sparse-GP architecture. The rotated stress–strain pairs are introduced specifically to encourage this relation during training. Thus, rotational consistency is exact for the invariant-driven latent transition but approximate and learned from augmented data for the tensorial stress map. It’s important to emphasize that the assumptions in this section would, of course, break down for a material with a fixed anisotropic microstructure, such as bedding planes, joint sets, or a preferred fabric orientation. In such cases, testing along a rotated axis would probe a genuinely different response that could not be recovered by rotating the original data.

sections.heading: 5.4 Training protocol
sections.text: Training is performed by minimizing the negative ELBO of Eq. ( 23 ) for the sparse multi-output GP together with the neural transition parameters, in the normalized form of Eq. ( 26 ), using a small number of cross-validation folds trained with different random seeds. Each fold uses a fixed, moderate number of inducing points, a bounded number of training epochs with early stopping on validation performance, a fixed learning rate, and the S S -sample Monte Carlo average over stochastic latent state rollouts defined in Eq. ( 28 ), evaluated on the downsampled training and validation sequences of Section 5.2 . The expected log-likelihood inside the ELBO is evaluated in the closed form given in Eq. ( 25 ). Exact hyperparameter values are reported in A . The best checkpoint is selected by autoregressive validation RMSE in normalized stress units. The corresponding optimization-time RMSE and epoch are reported in A . After checkpoint selection, the model is evaluated offline on the complete validation and test time histories in Section 6.1 before being exported for the finite element deployment cases in Sections 6.2 – 6.4 . In the next section, we first verify the learned constitutive relation against complete RVE-scale histories. We then test whether that relation can be exported to and correctly executed within a commercial finite element package (in this case Abaqus), from a single integration point to a multi-element structural simulation. Our objective is therefore verification of the learned material-point update and its implementation and deployment pathway in Abaqus/Explicit.

sections.heading: 6 Results
sections.text: We proceed through four cases of increasing complexity. Case 1 (Section 6.1 ) evaluates the trained GP-SSM on complete validation and test histories and therefore establishes the constitutive law prediction to be deployed, independently of its finite element implementation. Case 2 (Section 6.2 ) then documents the full Abaqus/Explicit deployment pathway, from the exported parameter file to the VUMAT update loop, and exercises it under a triaxial path in which the confining stress changes during loading. Case 3 (Section 6.3 ) extends the deployed material-point model to include an unloading–reloading rule that freezes the learned latent memory whenever the equivalent strain drops below its historical maximum, an ingredient required before structural simulation because some material points may unload while others continue to load to the softening regime. Case 4 (Section 6.4 ) uses that rule in a multi-element structural model that reproduces a loading condition from the KCC literature and compares the resulting structural compression response against the KCC model as a reference solution. In all cases, the GP-SSM is developed using N hist = 20 N_{\mathrm{hist}}=20 synthetic triaxial compression histories generated with the KCC model implemented as an Abaqus/Explicit VUMAT. The data-generation simulations follow the loading conditions used in Figure 4 of Wu and Crawford (2015) , with monotonic axial compression applied under fixed lateral confinement. The dataset spans confining pressures from 2 2 to 40 ​ MPa 40~\mathrm{MPa} , with each history recording the response to monotonic axial compression under fixed lateral confinement. These histories capture the initial loading branch, peak strength, and post-peak softening toward residual response, covering the transition from a sharp stress drop at low confinement to more gradual softening and higher sustained strength at elevated confinement. The data are partitioned by complete loading history: twelve sequences at 2 , 6 , 8 , 12 , 16 , 20 , 22 , 24 , 30 , 33 , 36 , 2,6,8,12,16,20,22,24,30,33,36, and 38 ​ MPa 38~\mathrm{MPa} are used for training, five at 10 , 14 , 18 , 31 , 10,14,18,31, and 40 ​ MPa 40~\mathrm{MPa} for validation, and three at 4 , 26 , 4,26, and 28 ​ MPa 28~\mathrm{MPa} for testing. The model learns from the strain and stress histories, with equivalent strain and stress invariants calculated from these quantities; KCC internal variables are not supplied as training targets. Each training sequence is reduced to 100 temporally aligned points after preprocessing, whereas the final validation and test evaluations use the complete preprocessed histories. Figure 3 summarizes the training dynamics for a representative fold. The negative-ELBO loss in Figure 3 (a) decreases rapidly during the initial epochs and then improves more gradually, approaching a plateau with small fluctuations. Figure 3 (b) shows a corresponding reduction in both training and validation RMSE. The validation error fluctuates more strongly because it is evaluated through closed-loop autoregressive rollout, whereas the training error uses reference previous-step stress invariants. After the initial improvement, further reductions in training loss yield limited gains in validation accuracy. The checkpoint at epoch 3100 is therefore selected using the exponentially moving average of the validation RMSE, with a normalized validation RMSE of approximately 0.0347 0.0347 , and is used for the subsequent evaluations and finite element deployment. Figure 3: Training dynamics of the GP-SSM (representative fold): (a) Negative-ELBO training loss versus epoch; (b) Train and validation RMSE evaluated every 100 epochs, where train RMSE is computed non-autoregressively on N tpts = 100 N_{\mathrm{tpts}}=100 downsampled points per sequence and validation RMSE uses closed-loop autoregressive rollout on N vpts = 500 N_{\mathrm{vpts}}=500 points per sequence, with predicted stress fed back as the invariants at each step. The marked point (epoch 3100) indicates the checkpoint selected by early stopping on the EMA-smoothed validation RMSE.

sections.heading: 6.1 Case 1: Offline full-sequence rollout evaluation
sections.text: Case 1 is performed offline with respect to the finite element package. After the checkpoint is selected using the optimization-time validation procedure of Section 5.4 , the model is evaluated on the complete preprocessed time history of every sequence shown in Figure 4 (the black dashed lines in the figure denote the reference RVE-scale stress histories). Neither the validation sequences nor the test sequences (yellow background in Figure 4 ) are temporally downsampled for this final evaluation. At each time step, the measured strain is supplied to the model, the latent state is advanced incrementally, and the predicted stress, rather than the reference stress, is used to compute the invariants supplied to the next step. The validation and test results are therefore closed-loop autoregressive rollouts over the full time series, and assess accumulated sequential prediction error rather than isolated one-step accuracy. Figure 4: Offline GP-SSM predictions of the axial stress–strain response under triaxial compression with reported levels of confinement, shown as | σ 11 | |\sigma_{11}| against | ϵ 11 | |\epsilon_{11}| for each confining pressure (labeled in MPa). Black dashed lines denote the reference RVE-scale stress histories. Solid blue lines denote the GP-SSM posterior mean, and the shaded bands show the 68% and 95% credible intervals. Training sequences (white background) are evaluated non-autoregressively using the reference previous-step stress invariants. Validation and test sequences (yellow background) are evaluated in closed-loop autoregressive rollout over their complete preprocessed time histories, without temporal downsampling, with predicted stress fed back to compute the invariants at the next step. RMSE and mean predictive standard deviation are reported for each sequence. As shown in Figure 4 , the model reproduces the systematic increase in peak and residual axial strength with confinement across the full set of RVE-scale histories. For the training sequences, the RMSE ranges from 1.04 1.04 to 2.32 ​ MPa 2.32~\mathrm{MPa} . More importantly for offline generalization, the full-sequence validation RMSE ranges from 1.86 1.86 to 4.04 ​ MPa 4.04~\mathrm{MPa} , and the test RMSE ranges from 1.73 1.73 to 3.20 ​ MPa 3.20~\mathrm{MPa} . The closest agreement occurs for the more highly confined test histories at 26 26 and 28 ​ MPa 28~\mathrm{MPa} , where the predicted curves track the reference loading, peak, softening, and residual response. The largest discrepancies occur at low confinement, particularly for the 10 ​ MPa 10~\mathrm{MPa} validation history and the 4 ​ MPa 4~\mathrm{MPa} test history, where the reference response exhibits a sharp post-peak stress drop that is represented by a smoother transition in the GP-SSM prediction. The predictive intervals also widen in these low-confinement cases, consistent with their greater rollout error. These results establish that the trained state-space update remains stable when rolled out over every point of a held-out sequence and interpolates across unseen confinement levels within the available triaxial loading family. They do not, by themselves, establish generalization to loading paths outside that family. Instead, Cases 2–4 test whether this offline constitutive update can be implemented and exercised correctly in finite element analyses.

sections.heading: 6.2 Deployment within finite element software
sections.text: Here, in Case 2, we make the complete pipeline explicit, from experimental data to a verified finite element deployment, shown in Figure 5 . Training uses only strain and stress histories that are directly measurable in a standard triaxial compression test, without measuring or prescribing damage, plastic strain, or any other internal variable. The latent state 𝒛 t \bm{z}_{t} that plays this role is instead inferred statistically, through the variational training procedure of Section 4 . The same inferred history representation, not a hand-specified damage or plasticity variable, advances the material state once the trained model is embedded in the finite element solver (in this case, Abaqus/Explicit). This experiment-to-deployment pipeline is exercised end-to-end for the first time in this Case 2. sections.heading: 6.2.1 Deployment protocol
sections.text: After training, the model parameters are exported through a lightweight parameter file representation. The exported parameter file contains the four affine layers of the transition network, the inducing-point matrix, ARD length scales, output scales, GP mean constants, posterior-mean coefficients, and normalization statistics. The exported representation is evaluated inside a VUMAT user material subroutine in Abaqus/Explicit, and Cases 2–4 execute through this same deployment pathway. This file-based representation is intentionally simple. The VUMAT reads the parameters once, stores them in local arrays, and performs only elementary floating-point operations during the material-point update. sections.heading: 6.3 Case 3: Unloading–reloading extension
sections.text: The RVE-scale histories evaluated in Case 1 and the finite element loading path in Case 2 are monotonic: equivalent strain never decreases, and the sign constraint of Eq. ( 19 ) means the latent state only accumulates. A structural simulation cannot be restricted to monotonic loading at every material point. Once some region of a structure begins to soften, deformation may localize into a narrow band while neighboring material points unload. For local strain-softening constitutive laws, this localization can lead to loss of well-posedness and mesh sensitivity. A substantial literature addresses this issue by introducing an internal length scale through crack-band models ( Bažant and Oh, 1983 ) , integral nonlocal damage ( Pijaudier-Cabot and Bažant, 1987 ; Bažant and Jirásek, 2002 ) , gradient-enhanced damage ( Peerlings et al., 1996 ) , phase-field fracture models ( Miehe et al., 2010 ) , and (most recently) a smooth crack band model (sCBM) using “sprain energy," which introduces the curvature of the displacement field as an explicit localization limiter ( Xu et al., 2024b ) . Reproducing these methods is not the objective of the present paper. Instead, Case 3 introduces a physically consistent elastic unloading branch for the material-point update, so that individual integration points can unload without violating the irreversibility built into the learned latent transition. This supplies the minimum ingredient needed to perform multi-element structural simulation. This unloading branch is built on the equivalent-strain memory already used to gate the extrapolation guard in Section 6.2 . Because 𝒛 t f \bm{z}_{t_{f}} retains learned information accumulated over the preceding loading history, it can serve the same functional role as classical internal or history variables used to represent damage, plastic strain, and related irreversible processes. This interpretation does not require assigning any individual latent coordinate a one-to-one physical meaning. The axial displacement remains zero during this confinement ramp and is then increased linearly to 25 ​ mm 25~\mathrm{mm} between t = 0.2 t=0.2 and 1.0 ​ s 1.0~\mathrm{s} . The analysis is performed with Abaqus/Explicit with geometric nonlinearity disabled. Every GP-SSM material point uses the frozen-memory elastic unloading rule of Section 6.3 , since the structural loading condition produces unloading in some elements while others continue to load. (a) axial reaction force versus imposed end displacement, with an inset showing the deformed mesh. (c) histogram of the final axial strain | E 11 | |E_{11}| at 25 ​ mm 25~\mathrm{mm} end displacement over all elements for the GP-SSM (blue) and KCC (orange) simulations. Figure 8 (a) shows that the GP-SSM closely tracks the full force-displacement relation of the KCC reference, including its initial stiffness, peak load, and softening. Its peak force is only 1.4 % 1.4\% higher and occurs about 1.6 ​ mm 1.6~\mathrm{mm} later, indicating a slightly more ductile pre-peak response. After the peak, the GP-SSM loses load-carrying capacity slightly faster and predicts a reaction force about 4.3 % 4.3\% lower at 25 ​ mm 25~\mathrm{mm} , suggesting stronger post-peak degradation or localization. Figure 8 (b) shows the element-wise axial stress–strain trajectories for both models. Before the peak, the KCC and GP-SSM trajectories nearly coincide. During post-peak softening, however, the KCC element responses (in orange) and the GP-SSP element responses differ. The same contrast appears in the distribution of the final elemental axial strains for the two models, shown in Fig. 8 (c). Both models leave most elements at the elastically unloaded value, but the KCC elements in the tail tend to fall into discrete clusters, while the GP-SSM counts form a single smooth tail with a slightly wider spread. Figure 8 (d) shows that this difference in local description does not change the deformation pattern. The GP-SSM band is slightly more intensely localized, consistent with the faster post-peak load drop in Fig. 8 (a). Two mechanisms contribute to the branching observed in Figure 8 (b) and (c). First, the KCC implementation regularizes softening using an element-size factor derived from the element volume relative to the prescribed localization width. Discrete element-size classes can therefore generate discrete softening slopes. Second, spatial variations in confinement and boundary restraint lead different integration points to distinct pressure histories and residual-strength states. The GP-SSM represents the response through 𝒛 \bm{z} , ε eq \varepsilon^{\mathrm{eq}} , the previous stress invariants I 1 I_{1} and J 2 J_{2} , and the six strain components. Element size and structural location are not included explicitly because the formulation targets a local material response learned from stress–strain histories rather than a mesh-dependent representation of the KCC branches. When multiple KCC response branches correspond to inputs that are indistinguishable within the current GP-SSM feature space, the Gaussian-likelihood GP cannot represent those branches separately; its posterior mean instead tends toward their conditional average. It consequently averages the KCC branches into a central band, as would a deterministic neural network trained with a squared-error loss. The structural force nevertheless remains accurate because it is a sequence of volume integrals of the element stresses (or energy), so branchwise deviations can balance through spatial averaging even when individual element paths are not recovered. The agreement of the force–displacement curves therefore shows that the volume-averaged response is represented accurately despite the different local descriptions of post-peak softening. Reproducing the individual KCC branches would constitute a different modeling objective and would require explicit structural descriptors or a multimodal output representation. These results support a simple conclusion: a latent state learned from stress–strain sequences alone, with no measured or prescribed internal variable, can be accurate and numerically stable enough to serve as the local history variable in a commercial explicit solver, from a single integration point up to a full structural response. Nothing in this formulation is specific to strain softening, moreover. The model assumes neither that strength degrades, nor that a peak exists, nor that deformation localizes. Its only material-specific commitments are the invariant descriptors chosen to drive the latent transition. The same structure therefore applies to any path-dependent material for which stress–strain histories can be recorded, including work-hardening and cyclically loaded metals and rate-dependent polymers, with the descriptor set adapted to the mechanisms that govern each.

sections.heading: 7.1 Latent state as learned constitutive history
sections.text: The primary conceptual contribution of our framework is the interpretation of the state-space latent variable as a learned constitutive history variable that is sufficient to make predictions of material response. Classical inelasticity introduces internal variables to make the stress depend on the past. The present model preserves that incremental structure, but learns the history representation implicitly from observable stress–strain sequences. This avoids prescribing a particular damage or plasticity variable while still providing the finite element solver with state variables that can be updated locally. The latent state should not be overinterpreted as a unique physical damage measure. Different latent coordinates may rotate, rescale, or mix without changing the stress prediction. Nevertheless, their monotonic evolution under loading, and their dependence on equivalent strain and stress invariants, make them useful low-dimensional summaries of irreversible loading history. The frozen-memory elastic unloading rule introduced in Case 3 (Section 6.3 ) completes this interpretation. Because the latent state is only allowed to evolve while equivalent strain increases, and is otherwise held fixed while the material point responds elastically, the state behaves as a genuine memory variable rather than a function of the instantaneous strain alone. In this sense, the model is closer to an internal-variable constitutive update than to a memoryless stress regressor.

sections.heading: 7.2 Relation to recurrent neural constitutive models
sections.text: The formulation differs from conventional gated recurrent constitutive surrogates based on long-short-term-memory (LSTM) or gated recurrent unit (GRU) architectures, in which increasing the width or depth of the recurrent architecture typically increases the dimension of the hidden state propagated between loading increments ( Mozaffar et al., 2019 ; Gorji et al., 2020 ) . Consequently, these models often employ recurrent state vectors with many hidden components whose individual coordinates generally have no prescribed mechanical interpretation. In the present formulation, the capacity of the transition network is decoupled from the dimension of the persistent material memory. The hidden-layer activations are discarded after each update, and only the two-dimensional latent state 𝐳 t \mathbf{z}_{t} is retained as the constitutive history variable. The two latent coordinates should not be interpreted as uniquely identified physical variables. Their evolution is nevertheless more mechanically structured than an unconstrained recurrent hidden state. Equivalent-strain progression determines when and by how much the state evolves, the softplus transition enforces monotonic accumulation, and the previous-step invariants I 1 I_{1} and J 2 J_{2} introduce pressure and deviatoric sensitivity. The current strain tensor is retained separately in the stress map, allowing invariant quantities to compress loading history without discarding the tensorial information required for stress prediction. The Minimal State Cell (MSC) and its self-consistent linearized extension (LMSC) approach ( Bonatti and Mohr, 2021 ; Bonatti and Mohr, 2022 ) decouples network capacity from persistent-state dimension and reduces sensitivity to loading-path discretization. In contrast, the present formulation expresses latent-state evolution through a mechanics-informed evolution law driven by invariant quantities, in which the learned transition represents an evolution rate that is scaled by the equivalent-strain increment. This construction follows the structure of classical internal-variable evolution equations more closely than a generic recurrent hidden-state update while retaining a learned latent representation. For this class of models, the latent dimension should be chosen as the smallest dimension that makes the constitutive update adequately Markovian. The number of state variables required by a conventional model representing similar material mechanisms can provide a useful initial reference, but does not imply a one-to-one correspondence. Too few latent variables may fail to distinguish materially different loading histories, whereas excessive dimensions introduce redundant, weakly identified and tightly coupled coordinates and may increase the risk of overfitting. Additional constraints, such as irreversibility and thermodynamic consistency expressed through nonnegative mechanical dissipation, can restrict the admissible space of latent evolutions. Related thermodynamics- and mechanics-informed architectures illustrate how such structure can be embedded in learned constitutive models and show improved robustness to noise and inputs outside the training domain ( Masi et al., 2021 ; As’ad et al., 2022 ) . Thus, the proposed approach offers numerous opportunities for growth and extensions to wide-ranging material classes with increasingly complex deformation mechanisms in the future. The GP stress map provides an additional distinction. Rather than using a deterministic neural network for all components of the constitutive update, the present model separates history evolution from stress prediction and employs a sparse multi-output Gaussian process to map the latent state and current strain tensor to the stress tensor. Besides its data efficiency, the GP retains an explicit posterior representation that can be used offline to assess epistemic uncertainty, identify extrapolation, and guide new data acquisition. The present VUMAT evaluates only the posterior mean because explicit finite-element analysis requires inexpensive local constitutive updates, but the probabilistic formulation remains valuable for model assessment. What makes the posterior useful in practice is its decomposition. As shown in Section 4.4 , the epistemic component measures distance from the training support and is the only contribution that additional experiments can reduce, whereas the likelihood noise is a fixed pedestal common to every sequence. Since this noise is the same for every loading path, it does not affect how paths compare, and the epistemic term alone ranks candidate experiments by how poorly the existing data support them. This ranking requires only the proposed state–strain query, so it can be computed before the experiment is performed. The model therefore supplies its own acquisition and quality criterion. New tests can be targeted where the posterior is widest rather than by uniform coverage or engineering intuition, and the same quantity flags when a structural calculation leaves training regime. Note that this capability is absent from the fixed-form alternative. A least-squares calibration of the KCC strength surfaces returns a single parameter set and no internal measure of where that set is unsupported. As C shows, the calibration data are reproduced by the KCC model about equally well by a whole family of parameter sets rather than by one, so which member the fit returns is settled by the optimiser and the starting point. The resulting model does not describe this ambiguity, and reports the same unqualified confidence everywhere it is subsequently evaluated. Adding experiments does not systematically reduce this ambiguity, because the residual reflects the assumed functional form rather than a lack of data. The learned formulation instead reports where it is uninformed and improves in exactly those regions when data are supplied, which is the practical value of carrying uncertainty through the constitutive model.

sections.heading: 7.3 Limitations and future work
sections.text: Because this finite element deployment uses an explicit dynamic algorithm, the lateral stress response at low confinement is inherently less numerically stable, a characteristic of explicit dynamic time integration rather than of the learned constitutive update itself. Since the training histories were assembled to characterize behavior under moderate-to-high confinement, they do not specifically target this low-pressure regime, and predictive accuracy there is correspondingly expected to be weaker and warrants further investigation. In addition, the elastic unloading rule of Case 3 is a minimal, non-learned closure. It freezes the latent memory and reuses the initial elastic stiffness rather than learning an unloading/reloading stiffness directly from data, and it does not represent nonlinear unloading behavior such as material hysteresis or the stiffness softening caused by crack propagation. Future work could further strengthen the physical interpretation of the latent variables by coupling the GP-SSM to multiscale modeling frameworks. Lower-scale simulations could provide information on mechanisms such as microcrack growth, frictional sliding, and plastic deformation, allowing the latent representation to be learned jointly from macroscopic stress–strain histories and microstructural descriptors. Additional consistency constraints could link latent evolution to these mechanisms and their contributions to the macroscopic response. This would extend the present interpretation of the latent state as accumulated material memory toward a representation informed by processes across scales. The framework could also be extended to other material classes, including viscoelastic polymers and viscoplastic metals. For rate-dependent materials, the latent transition could incorporate physical time, strain rate, and temperature, with evolution integrated over the physical time increment. This would allow the state to evolve during sustained loading and strain holds, providing a route to representing creep, stress relaxation, and rate-sensitive yielding. The latent evolution rules could be tailored to the relevant mechanisms, combining monotonic components for irreversible accumulation with signed components for recoverable processes. Training histories spanning different loading rates, hold durations, and temperatures would support the identification and validation of these extensions.

sections.heading: 8 Conclusions
sections.text: This study develops a general GP-SSM framework for modeling the path-dependent mechanical response of rate-independent materials and applies the approach to finite element modeling of quasi-brittle materials. By learning latent history variables through variational inference and constraining their evolution with mechanics-informed structure, the framework constructs an incremental constitutive model using only observable stress–strain quantities. The principal features are: 1. The framework constructs a path-dependent constitutive model entirely from observable quantities. Variational inference learns a latent representation of material history directly from stress–strain sequences, eliminating the need to prescribe or measure model-specific damage, plastic-strain, or hardening variables. 2. Mechanics-informed structure turns the learned state into a compact constitutive memory. The two-dimensional state evolves through a nonnegative rate scaled by equivalent-strain progression and conditioned on the pressure and deviatoric invariants I 1 I_{1} and J 2 J_{2} . This construction suppresses spurious drift, enforces cumulative evolution during loading, and decouples the dimension of the persistent material state from the capacity of the transition network. Retaining the current strain tensor in the stress map further preserves the full tensorial information needed for six-component stress prediction. 3. The sparse GP stress map accurately reproduces held-out sequential responses while retaining probabilistic information. Full-sequence closed-loop rollouts captured the confinement-dependent loading, peak, softening, and residual behavior. The predictive intervals widened in the more difficult low-confinement cases, demonstrating how the GP posterior can complement point predictions with an internal indicator of data support and extrapolation risk. 4. The learned constitutive update can be implemented into a lightweight, self-contained Abaqus/Explicit material model. The exported evaluator requires no machine-learning library and advances only local state variables at each integration point. Under a changing-confinement path not included in training, the VUMAT tracked the pressure increase and reproduced the response from traditional model through peak and post-peak softening. This establishes a complete route from observable material data to an incrementally evaluated finite element constitutive law. 5. The state-space formulation extends naturally from material-point loading to unloading and structural response. Freezing the latent memory below the historical maximum equivalent strain preserves irreversible history while allowing stable unloading–reloading. More significantly, the structural simulation shows that a constitutive update learned solely from material-point histories transfers to a structural boundary-value problem without any training on structural force–displacement data. This scale transfer is the essential requirement for a data-driven constitutive law to be of practical use in engineering analysis, since it allows a model calibrated with element-level material tests to be applied directly to structural components. 6. The framework provides a modular foundation for broader data-driven constitutive modeling. Its transition law, probabilistic stress map, and finite element deployment are separable components that can be extended independently. Further, because the formulation itself is agnostic to the specific physics of quasi-brittle damage, the same latent-state architecture extends naturally to other history-dependent material classes, including rate-independent and rate-dependent plasticity and viscoelastic or viscoplastic polymers, by retraining on the corresponding stress–strain histories and adapting the invariant conditioning to the governing physics of each material class. 7. Strain localization can be treated separately from the learned local constitutive response. Localization may be controlled through a material-point or element-size-dependent regularization, or through a field-coupled nonlocal or gradient formulation. In the present structural verification, the GP-SSM captured the global force–displacement response even though the statistical distributions of element-level stress–strain trajectories may differ. The global structural response and the local trajectory ensemble are therefore complementary validation targets: the former reflects the integrated load-carrying behavior, whereas the latter depends on the particular constitutive and localization design. These results demonstrate the principal advantages of the proposed approach. It learns constitutive history from observable data, embeds that history in a compact and mechanically structured state, retains a probabilistic measure of model support, and produces a local update suitable for finite element calculations. The framework thereby connects state-space learning with the internal-variable structure of classical constitutive mechanics while reducing the need for prescribed phenomenological history variables.

sections.heading: Appendix C Non-uniqueness of strength-surface calibration
sections.text: Figure 9: Non-uniqueness of the KCC maximum-surface calibration. (a) Fits of Δ ​ σ m ​ ( p ) \Delta\sigma_{m}(p) (Eq. ( 2 )) to twenty M7 peak triaxial strengths (circles), each fixing a 0 a_{0} at the value shown and refitting the rest; parentheses give the RMS residual relative to the optimum ( 0.69 0.69 MPa). Values of a 0 a_{0} spanning nearly an order of magnitude fit the data almost equally well, separating only below about 10 10 MPa. (b) RMS residual over the ( a 0 , a 2 ) (a_{0},a_{2}) plane, with the optimum (star) and the contour at twice its residual (red), which encloses the fits of (a): a long correlated valley rather than an isolated minimum, since a 0 a_{0} and 1 / a 2 1/a_{2} are constrained mainly through the asymptote a 0 + 1 / a 2 a_{0}+1/a_{2} . Section 2.4 argued that the elastic predictor is essentially free while the boundary function must be designed from phenomenology. This appendix makes that cost concrete for the maximum surface Δ ​ σ m ​ ( p ) \Delta\sigma_{m}(p) of Eq. ( 2 ), fitted by nonlinear least squares to twenty triaxial peak strengths generated with the microplane model M7 ( Caner and Bažant, 2013a ; Caner and Bažant, 2013b ) , for a concrete calibrated to the same unconfined compressive strength, elastic modulus, and Poisson’s ratio as the material of Section 6 ( k 1 = 87.35 × 10 − 6 k_{1}=87.35\times 10^{-6} , E = 30448.2 E=30448.2 MPa, and ν = 0.19 \nu=0.19 ). The intent is not to argue that KCC model cannot represent this “new type” of material, but that even the most favourable step of its calibration (three parameters, a directly observable target, no time integration) is already ill-posed. The fit shown in Fig. 9 (a) looks normal. The fitted surface passes through the twenty peak strengths across the whole range of mean pressures tested, with a root-mean-square residual of 0.69 0.69 MPa, and no systematic departure is visible anywhere along the curve. Judged as it would ordinarily be judged, by how closely the calibrated surface reproduces the data it was fitted to, the calibration is successful. What the figure cannot show is that the parameter set producing this curve is poorly determined. The three coefficients are strongly correlated: as p → ∞ p\to\infty , Eq. ( 2 ) approaches the finite asymptote a 0 + 1 / a 2 a_{0}+1/a_{2} , so a 0 a_{0} and 1 / a 2 1/a_{2} enter the high-pressure response only through their sum and can be exchanged almost freely unless the data extend far enough to constrain that asymptote, which lies well beyond the largest pressure tested here. The least-squares objective therefore has no isolated minimum but a long curved valley of parameter sets, shown in Fig. 9 (b), spanning nearly an order of magnitude in a 0 a_{0} , every one of which reproduces the data in Fig. 9 (a) about as closely as the curve plotted. Their predictions coincide over the calibrated range and diverge widely outside it. Nor is this resolved by collecting more data at the same pressures: the residual at the optimum is systematic model-form discrepancy rather than measurement scatter, so additional measurements force a compromise across it instead of refining the estimate. This is the phenomenological cost of Section 2.4 made quantitative, and it is a property of fitting a rigid functional form to data of limited range, not a defect specific to KCC. The GP-SSM developed in this paper does not avoid this by having fewer parameters; indeed, it has substantially more. What changes is that they are inferred by variational inference directly from observed stress–strain sequences, so an additional experiment tightens a well-posed optimisation rather than adding a further target to a manual search over a flat, correlated objective. No surface is designed or tabulated in advance. The posterior variance further reports where the model is unsupported by data, which a calibrated fixed-form surface does not provide.

sections.heading: Appendix D Training Data Generation
sections.text: Synthetic stress–strain histories were generated from single-element tests. These tests were simulated in Abaqus/Explicit using the Karagozian and Case Concrete (KCC) Release III model, implemented through a user-defined VUMAT. These simulations provide controlled reference responses for learning the dependence of stress on strain and loading history under different confinement levels. The specimen was represented by a cube with an initial side length of 101.6 ​ mm 101.6~\mathrm{mm} , discretized using one eight-node, reduced-integration solid element (C3D8R) with enhanced hourglass control. Geometric nonlinearity was enabled. On each of the three coordinate planes x i = 0 x_{i}=0 , the normal velocity component was constrained to zero, while tangential motion remained unconstrained. The single integration point provided a material-point stress–strain history for each prescribed loading condition. The material parameters were held fixed across the simulations. The density was 2321 ​ kg / m 3 2321~\mathrm{kg/m^{3}} , the unconfined compressive strength was f c ′ = 45.2 ​ MPa f_{c}^{\prime}=45.2~\mathrm{MPa} , and Poisson’s ratio was ν = 0.19 \nu=0.19 . The specified bulk and shear moduli were K = 16.37 ​ GPa K=16.37~\mathrm{GPa} and G = 12.79 ​ GPa G=12.79~\mathrm{GPa} , respectively. The localization width used by the KCC regularization was 48 ​ mm 48~\mathrm{mm} . The automatic parameter-generation option for normal-weight concrete supplied the remaining unspecified constitutive parameters. Strain-rate enhancement was disabled, so the reference constitutive response did not include rate-dependent strength amplification. Each simulation followed a two-stage loading protocol. During the first stage, equal compressive pressures were applied to the three faces opposite the constrained coordinate planes and increased smoothly from zero to the target confining pressure p c p_{c} over 0.20 ​ s 0.20~\mathrm{s} . During the second stage, these pressures were maintained, and additional axial compression was imposed by prescribing the velocity of the face initially located at x 1 = 101.6 ​ mm x_{1}=101.6~\mathrm{mm} . The axial velocity increased smoothly in magnitude from zero at t = 0.20 ​ s t=0.20~\mathrm{s} to 25.4 ​ mm / s 25.4~\mathrm{mm/s} at t = 0.30 ​ s t=0.30~\mathrm{s} , after which it remained constant. This velocity corresponds to a nominal axial strain-rate magnitude of 0.25 ​ s − 1 0.25~\mathrm{s}^{-1} , based on the initial specimen length. The second stage lasted 0.40 ​ s 0.40~\mathrm{s} , giving a total analysis duration of 0.60 ​ s 0.60~\mathrm{s} . Different stress-strain histories were obtained by varying the prescribed confinement p c p_{c} . Stress and strain were recorded directly within the VUMAT at successive constitutive updates, including both elastic and inelastic loading. The strain tensor was calculated from the deformation gradient as 𝐄 = 1 2 ​ ( 𝐅 𝖳 ​ 𝐅 − 𝐈 ) , \mathbf{E}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\mathbf{F}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{F}-\mathbf{I}\right), (42) and paired with the updated Cauchy stress tensor after the constitutive correction and restoration of the hydrostatic stress contribution. Thus, the exported strains are Green–Lagrange strains, and the exported stresses are total stresses. All six independent components were retained in the order 11 , 22 , 33 , 12 , 23 , 13 11,22,33,12,23,13 , with tensorial shear strains. Although the output also contained KCC internal variables and constitutive moduli, the GP-SSM used only the strain–stress histories and descriptors calculated from them; KCC internal variables were not used as training targets. The resulting dataset comprised 20 triaxial compression histories spanning confining pressures from 2 2 to 40 ​ MPa 40~\mathrm{MPa} . These histories covered initial loading, peak strength, and subsequent softening toward the residual response. Complete histories were assigned to separate training, validation, and test sets. Twelve histories at 2 , 6 , 8 , 12 , 16 , 20 , 22 , 24 , 30 , 33 , 36 , 2,6,8,12,16,20,22,24,30,33,36, and 38 ​ MPa 38~\mathrm{MPa} were used for training; five at 10 , 14 , 18 , 31 , 10,14,18,31, and 40 ​ MPa 40~\mathrm{MPa} for validation; and three at 4 , 26 , 4,26, and 28 ​ MPa 28~\mathrm{MPa} for testing. This partition evaluates prediction at confinement levels absent from training while preserving the sequential structure of each loading history. Subsequent preprocessing, normalization, temporal downsampling, and rotational augmentation are described in Section 5 .

Shields Affiliation: Hopkins Extreme Materials Institute, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD, USA Affiliation: Department of Civil and Systems Engineering, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD, USA Abstract Constitutive models for history-dependent, path-dependent materials typically encode this dependence in prescribed functional forms through internal variables such as damage or plastic strain that are phenomenological, model-dependent, and not directly observable. These rigid functional forms lack flexibility to match observations, make calibration potentially non-unique, and complicate uncertainty quantification and propagation through finite element predictions. This paper develops a Gaussian-process state-space model (GP-SSM) that replaces the fixed form of the constitutive model with a flexible GP regression, and the prescribed internal variables with a set of latent state variables learned directly from observable stress–strain histories. As a GP, the model is naturally endowed with a measure of uncertainty and can be constrained to satisfy necessary physical principles. We demonstrate this framework for quasi-brittle materials under triaxial compression, where the latent variable evolution is driven by the current-state stress invariants and the increment of equivalent strain to reflect the evolution of irreversible, pressure-sensitive history. A sparse multi-output Gaussian process then maps the latent state and current strain tensor to the six-component stress response. Variational sparse inference enables tractable training from sequential stress-strain data that retains a probabilistic structure for offline uncertainty assessment. The trained model is exported into Abaqus/Explicit through a user material subroutine. Four verification cases are reported: (1) offline full-sequence rollout evaluation on the validation and test histories; (2) a single element simulation under changing confinement, which exercises the complete Abaqus/Explicit deployment pathway; (3) a frozen-memory unloading–reloading extension in which latent evolution stops once equivalent strain recedes below its historical maximum; and (4) a multi-element structural model that reproduces a loading condition from the Karagozian and Case Concrete (KCC) model and is compared directly against KCC as a reference solution. These results show that the learned state-space update (i) reproduces held-out RVE-scale histories in closed-loop rollout, (ii) can be evaluated incrementally in an explicit finite element solver, (iii) tracks a confining stress that evolves during loading, (iv) supports unloading without violating the irreversibility of the learned history state, and (v) reproduces structural-level compression behavior consistent with an established constitutive model. The framework provides a practical route to bring together probabilistic machine learning, latent internal-state modeling, and finite element-compatible constitutive modeling. Keywords: Gaussian process state-space model , data-driven constitutive modeling , latent state variables , path dependence , quasi-brittle materials , finite element implementation 1 Introduction Path-dependent, history-dependent constitutive behavior is difficult to model because the current stress depends not only on the current strain but on the loading path. Classical phenomenological models, including damage mechanics, plasticity, and cap-type formulations, have hypothesized functional forms that represent this path dependence through internal variables whose predictive capability depends strongly on parameters that are difficult to identify uniquely from limited tests. This difficulty is especially pronounced for quasi-brittle materials such as concrete and rock ( Bažant and Planas, 1998 ; Yang et al., 2025 ) , where the macroscopic response is governed by evolving microcracking, frictional sliding, compaction, dilatancy, and confinement-dependent failure. These mechanisms produce nonlinear stiffness degradation, pressure-sensitive strength, path dependence, and post-peak softening. Cap-type formulations such as the Karagozian and Case Concrete (KCC) model ( Malvar et al., 1997 ; Wu and Crawford, 2015 ) have been widely adopted for this material class because they encode mechanics-inspired assumptions and are computationally efficient in finite element solvers, although (like other phenomenological models) they inherit the same difficulty of calibration. The central difficulty is not only that material parameters are uncertain. The internal history variables used by many constitutive theories are not directly measurable in standard stress–strain experiments. Quantities such as damage, plastic strain, hardening, crack-density, or compaction are introduced to make the constitutive update path dependent, but despite their physical interpretability, these variables as typically defined are model-specific and difficult to measure. As a result, calibration often becomes an ill-posed inverse problem: different parameter sets and internal-variable evolutions may reproduce the same observed stress–strain curves while implying different predictions under other loading paths. Replacing such fixed-form models and their prescribed internal variables with a representation learned directly from stress–strain data has a substantial history, dating back to early neural-network constitutive models ( Ghaboussi et al., 1991 ) . Deep-learning surrogates have also been applied directly to confinement-dependent, strain-softening rock behavior under triaxial loading ( Shi et al., 2022 ) . Recent surveys catalog the breadth of data-driven constitutive laws across material classes ( Fuhg et al., 2025 ) . A comprehensive review of these models is beyond the scope of this work. The need for a history-dependent representation of the material state is particularly important for quasi-brittle materials under triaxial compression. Confinement can change both stiffness and strength, while deviatoric loading controls shear-dominated damage and post-peak evolution. Two material points with the same instantaneous strain tensor may therefore correspond to different crack, compaction, and stress-history states. A data-driven material law that predicts stress only from the current strain tensor is unlikely to be robust when embedded in a finite element analysis, where local loading paths are generated by the coupled boundary-value problem rather than prescribed directly from laboratory tests. State-space learning provides a natural way to address this problem. Since the classical Kalman filter ( Kalman, 1960 ) , state-space models have introduced a hidden state that evolves incrementally and summarizes the information needed to predict a system’s future observations; Gaussian-process (GP) and recurrent neural-network extensions of this idea have been used to learn nonlinear latent dynamics directly from sequential data ( Wang et al., 2008 ; Krishnan et al., 2017 ) . In a constitutive setting, such a hidden state can be interpreted as a learned low-dimensional representation of the material history. Note that the hidden state need not be identifiable as the damage, plastic strain, or any particular classical or hypothesized internal variable. However, it serves the same functional role, encoding the essential information from the past that is needed to update the current stress. Moreover, essential physical constraints (e.g. non-negative dissipation) can be placed on these latent variables, and their interpretation may provide important mechanistic insights into material performance. In a related effort, recent work has begun to replace individual phenomenological surfaces within classical concrete models with data-driven models. Li et al. (2026) replace the empirical failure surface of the KCC model with a physics-constrained GP regression surrogate trained on triaxial compression data, and show that embedding known material-property constraints into the GP prior markedly improves accuracy (compared with an unconstrained regressor) and reduces predictive uncertainty and inadmissible material behavior beyond the training confinement range. That work uses a surrogate that replaces a single static failure surface evaluated at a given loading state. This paper develops a Gaussian-process state-space model (GP-SSM) formulation for history-dependent constitutive modeling. The model is specifically applied in the context of quasi-brittle materials, but the framework can be applied broadly to diverse classes of nonlinear history-dependent materials. The model combines three ingredients. First, a low-dimensional latent state represents unobserved material history. In conventional recurrent neural-network surrogates for path-dependent plasticity, the hidden vector plays two roles simultaneously: it propagates the material history forward from one increment to the next, and its size also determines how complex an update the network can represent. A more capable surrogate therefore requires a larger stored state, and such models commonly use comparatively large hidden states ( Mozaffar et al., 2019 ; Gorji et al., 2020 ) . The Minimal State Cell of Bonatti and Mohr (2021) was designed to separate these two roles, so that a wide and deep update network can act on a persistent state of only a few variables. Our model shares this state-parsimony objective. Its persistent memory is restricted to a small, fixed number of latent variables learned directly from stress–strain histories rather than prescribed as phenomenological internal variables. Its distinction lies in combining this compact state with a mechanics-informed evolution. The latent variable evolution is driven by equivalent strain and previous-step stress invariants, introducing mechanics-informed sensitivity to irreversible loading progression, pressure, and deviatoric stress intensity. Then, a sparse multi-output Gaussian process ( Rasmussen and Williams, 2005 ; Álvarez et al., 2012 ) , trained via stochastic variational inference over inducing points ( Titsias, 2009 ; Hensman et al., 2013 ) , maps the latent state and current strain tensor to the six-component stress tensor. This is in contrast to deterministic neural-network stress maps, and follows the general precedent of using Gaussian processes to model latent dynamical systems ( Deisenroth et al., 2015 ) . The Gaussian-process structure provides a nonparametric and data-efficient stress map built from a probabilistic formulation for quantifying uncertainty in the material model and allows offline uncertainty propagation through finite element simulations. A practical objective of this work is finite element compatibility. Data-driven constitutive models are frequently developed and validated as offline regressors. History-dependent machine-learning surrogates that have been embedded directly in finite element solvers have primarily been applied to accelerating multiscale FE 2 homogenization by, e.g., replacing an expensive micro-scale solve with a recurrent-neural-network surrogate ( Ghavamian and Simone, 2019 ) , or by using a trained recurrent network as the homogenized material update itself ( Logarzo et al., 2021 ) . This work demonstrates a full experiment-to-deployment pipeline built as an alternative to phenomenological constitutive models, in which the material model is evaluated locally and incrementally at every integration point, with state variables stored and updated by the solver. Note that although the verification cases in this paper use concrete-like triaxial data and are compared against the KCC model, the mechanics-informed state-space structure of GP-SSM is applicable to other pressure-sensitive, path-dependent quasi-brittle materials such as rocks and ceramics, that share the same broad failure mechanisms ( Bažant and Planas, 1998 ; Li and Ramesh, 2021 ) . Finally, Sections 7 and 8 discuss limitations and conclusions. 2 Background: constitutive modeling paradigms 2.1 Mechanistic, phenomenological, and data-driven modeling Constructing a constitutive model requires developing the stress–strain relation, and its history dependence. Three broad approaches are used in practice. Mechanistic models derive the relation from an explicit subscale mechanism. Phenomenological models instead postulate the relation at the scale of application and calibrate it to fit observed response, without deriving it directly from a lower-scale mechanism. Data-driven models learn the relation directly from stress–strain data, with minimal or no assumed functional form. These labels classify the origins of a modeling approach rather than the model that contains it. A complete constitutive model is typically a composite: it may derive one component from a mechanism, postulate a second, and (particularly recently) learn a third. The three approaches also differ in how much structure is assumed before any data are seen, and that choice involves a consistent trade-off. The more structure a model assumes, the less data it requires and the further it can be trusted outside the conditions on which it was calibrated, but the more its predictions depend on that structure being correct. The mechanistic paradigm is broadly applicable, but any individual mechanistic model is necessarily specific to the material class whose deformation mechanism it encodes. In metals, crystal plasticity derives macroscopic flow directly from dislocation slip on crystallographic slip systems ( Roters et al., 2010 ; Roters et al., 2019 ) . In polymers and elastomers, network theories such as the Arruda–Boyce eight-chain model derive the hyperelastic stress–stretch relation from the statistical mechanics of a network of freely jointed polymer chains ( Arruda and Boyce, 1993 ) . In both cases, the relation follows as a consequence of the assumed lower-scale mechanism rather than as a curve fit to test data, and in both cases the resulting model inherits the scope of that mechanism: slip kinematics has no counterpart in an elastomer network, and vice versa. The mechanistic route is therefore available only where the governing mechanism is both identified and tractably represented at the scale of interest. Phenomenological constitutive models have likewise been developed for a variety of material classes. Mooney–Rivlin hyperelasticity postulates a strain-energy function directly in terms of invariants of the deformation and calibrates its coefficients to (for example) rubber test data ( Mooney, 1940 ; Rivlin, 1948 ) , without deriving that function from a network mechanism. J 2 J_{2} (von Mises) plasticity with isotropic or kinematic hardening postulates a yield surface and hardening law for metals and calibrates them to observed hardening curves ( Lubliner, 2008 ; Simo and Hughes, 1998 ) , without necessarily deriving them from the mechanics of dislocation slip. The boundary between the mechanistic and phenomenological approaches may be softer than the definitions suggest. A postulated form is rarely arbitrary: e.g., J 2 J_{2} plasticity assumes that yielding is insensitive to pressure and to the third invariant, an assumption that is mechanistic in origin, since dislocation slip is volume-preserving. What makes such a model phenomenological is not the absence of mechanistic reasoning, but that the mechanism informs the choice of form rather than supplying it. This mixed character is apparent, for example, in damage or porosity-based constitutive models such as the Gurson-Tvergaard-Needleman (GTN) model ( Gurson, 1977 ; Tvergaard, 1981 ; Tvergaard and Needleman, 1984 ) that hypothesize a pressure-dependent yield function that is porosity dependent and phenomenologically informed by the mechanisms of void nucleation, growth, and coalescence. Data-driven constitutive models learn the relation, or its evolution, directly from observed data (whether measured or generated by simulation) with little or no assumed functional form. Such models differ among themselves chiefly in what is learned. Sequence models learn the incremental update itself, mapping strain history to stress through a recurrent hidden state ( Ghaboussi et al., 1991 ; Mozaffar et al., 2019 ; Gorji et al., 2020 ; Bonatti and Mohr, 2021 ) . Potential-based approaches learn a stored-energy or dissipation function and recover stress by differentiation, so that the learned object is a scalar rather than the stress ( Masi et al., 2021 ; As’ad et al., 2022 ) . Discovery-based approaches learn a sparse, interpretable expression for the law itself, in some cases from full-field displacement and reaction data without stress labels ( Flaschel et al., 2022 ) . Model-free data-driven computing dispenses with a constitutive function altogether, searching a database of observed states ( Kirchdoerfer and Ortiz, 2016 ) or their distribution ( Xu et al., 2024a ) directly; it is less a way of constructing a constitutive relation than a reformulation of the boundary-value problem that avoids needing one. Fuhg et al. (2025) survey this landscape across material classes in far more detail than is attempted here. The microplane model M7 ( Caner and Bažant, 2013a ; Caner and Bažant, 2013b ) illustrates the composite character of practical models. Its kinematic constraint decomposes strain onto a predefined set of microplane orientations and recovers the macroscopic stress through the principle of virtual work. This component is mechanistic, reflecting a geometric description of how the material transmits stress across orientations. The ‘boundary’ functions that bound the admissible normal and shear stresses on each microplane, however, do not follow from the kinematic constraint. Their functional forms and parameters are selected to reproduce observed uniaxial, biaxial, and triaxial responses. In the terminology used here, these functions provide the phenomenological component of the model. The same pattern recurs in the KCC model ( Malvar et al., 1997 ; Malvar et al., 2000 ; Wu et al., 2012 ; Wu and Crawford, 2015 ) and in LDPM ( Cusatis et al., 2011b ; Cusatis et al., 2011a ) . An explicit structural hypothesis (a pressure-dependent invariant space for KCC, particle geometry and contact kinematics for LDPM) is combined with strength or boundary functions calibrated against experimental data. Hybridization also occurs on the data-driven side. A learned component can be incorporated into a mechanistic model, for example by replacing the microplane boundary functions with a learned surrogate while retaining the kinematic constraint and virtual-work recovery. Alternatively, a learned model can keep the structural skeleton of a phenomenological model (an internal variable, an evolution law, and a stress response) while declining to specify any of them in closed form. Learned models are also routinely constrained to satisfy general mechanical requirements: a convex learned potential yields a hyperelastic, materially stable stress ( As’ad et al., 2022 ) ; invariant inputs enforce frame indifference and material symmetry ( Heider et al., 2020 ; Vlassis et al., 2020 ) ; a sign-constrained evolution enforces irreversibility and nonnegative dissipation ( Masi et al., 2021 ) . Constraints of this kind are not themselves a form of hybridization. Every constitutive model, in all three paradigms, is required to satisfy them. They restrict which relations are admissible, not where a relation originates. In this work, no boundary function is postulated and no return-mapping correction is performed. The stress update itself is learned as a nonparametric map from the current strain and an internal state to the current stress; whatever admissible region the material obeys is therefore implicit in that learned map under physics constraints. What the formulation retains from the models above is their structural skeleton rather than a derivation from any particular mechanism. It is mechanics-informed: the descriptors that drive the state are frame-invariant and the history they accumulate is irreversible. Section 2.4 makes this positioning precise. 2.2 Constitutive models for quasi-brittle materials Although the method is general, this paper focuses on quasi-brittle materials such as concrete and rock, for which the phenomenological paradigm has long been the dominant approach. A related pattern appears in the Lattice Discrete Particle Model (LDPM) ( Cusatis et al., 2011b ; Cusatis et al., 2011a ) , a meso-scale formulation that represents concrete as an assembly of rigid particles connected through lattice facets rather than as a continuum. As with KCC and the microplane model, the elastic response is evaluated first, and the facet-level state is subsequently mapped back onto a boundary surface designed and calibrated in advance. 2.4 The phenomenological cost of designing the boundary function Equations ( 2 ) and ( 3 ) exemplify what is implicit in most classical inelastic constitutive models: the elastic predictor in Eq. ( 1 ) is essentially free, but the boundary function that performs the correction must be designed almost entirely from phenomenology. In the case of the KCC model, the three independent pressure-dependent surfaces, a tension/compression-sensitive damage-accumulation rule, a fitted interpolation function η ⁡ ( λ ) \eta(\lambda) , and a separately calibrated rate-dependence curve together require a substantial battery of triaxial, uniaxial, and rate-dependent calibration tests, as well as engineering judgment about the functional forms in Eqs. ( 2 )–( 3 ) themselves and all of the underlying rules. Once fitted, the resulting boundary is tied to the assumed rational and piecewise functional forms, and its predictions away from the calibration database depend on how well those assumed forms extrapolate rather than on a quantity learned directly from data or underlying mechanisms that are known to govern in the extrapolation region. Other constitutive frameworks replace the three KCC surfaces with a cap surface, a Drucker–Prager cone, a continuum damage variable, a set of microplane boundary functions, or lattice-facet strength domains, but the underlying task is the same: the admissible-stress boundary and its history dependence must be explicitly designed, using a chosen functional form and a calibration campaign suited to that form, before the elastic-predictor, boundary-correction update can be used. This difficulty motivates the alternative approach pursued in this paper. Instead of committing in advance to a particular family of pressure-dependent strength surfaces and a fitted damage-interpolation function, the present model lets a latent state and a nonparametric Gaussian-process stress map absorb the analogous role, that of compressing irreversible loading history into quantities that modulate the current stress response directly from observed stress–strain sequences. The boundary-correction logic of Eqs. ( 2 ) and ( 3 ) is not imposed architecturally. Instead, the goal is to test whether a comparable pressure- and history-sensitive constitutive response can be learned through dependence on a small set of latent state variables, without prescribing the surfaces themselves. In the terms of Section 2.1 , this places the present work in the data-driven paradigm. What distinguishes it within that paradigm is how much it deliberately retains from the phenomenological one: a set of internal variables that record loading history, an evolution law driven by a scalar measure of loading progress, and a stress response modulated by the current value of those variables. What it declines to retain is the closed-form specification of each of those ingredients. This approach is developed for broad classes of materials that are rate-independent and path-dependent, as described in Section 4 . It is narrowed to quasi-brittle response only through the specific descriptor and irreversibility choices of Sections 3.4 and 4.2 . 3 Latent-state constitutive approach 3.1 Problem statement This section describes the learning problem, specifically defining the internal state variable and the associated evolution law that are inferred from observed stress–strain sequences as well as specifying the information that is assumed to be available for that inference. In Section 3.4 , the specific choice of 𝝃 t \bm{\xi}_{t} is then specified for the quasi-brittle materials studied here. 3.2 The use of a latent state A state-space model is a commonly used tool in controls, system identification, and other fields to represents a dynamical system by an internal state that evolves over time and (together with the current input) determines both the next state and the current observation ( Kalman, 1960 ; Särkkä, 2013 ) . The central premise of this representation is that the observation alone is generally not sufficient to predict the future of the system: two systems can share an identical current observation and yet be in different states, and therefore evolve differently from that point onward. Although historically it has not been posed in this way mathematically, the problem of constitutive modeling can be viewed through the state-space formalism. Two material points can be observed at the same instant with an identical current strain 𝜺 t \bm{\varepsilon}_{t} , yet they may have accumulated different histories of damage, plastic strain, or micro-cracking at the micro-, meso-, or macroscale, over the loading paths that produced that strain. These internal quantities are not directly measurable in a standard stress–strain test, yet they are critical to understanding the evolution of the material with deformation. A constitutive law therefore cannot be a memoryless map from strain to stress. Of course this is well-understood in the materials modeling field. The distinction here is that classical constitutive theories supply this representation explicitly, through prescribed damage or plastic-strain variables. The state-space formulation pursued in this work instead treats it as an implicit state to be learned. 3.3 Markov structure and probabilistic factorization The state-space formulation of Eq.
